  )





Figure 5: Weekly event-type heatmap. The steady baseline of check_email and assign_agent_task stands in contrast to the early-May spike in queue_subordinate_task (worm propagation).






3.6 SaidIT Permission Surface: How Wide Was the Worm’s Potential Target Set?
Before reconstructing the exact attack chain, a critical baseline question must be answered: how many agents in the system hold SaidIT posting permissions? The saidit_post_check event records every instance of an agent querying whether it is authorised to post. Any agent that appears here is a potential terminal executor for the worm - not just John Windward.


Show code
agent_worm_status <- bind_rows(
  chain_events %>% transmute(agent = sender,   in_chain = TRUE),
  chain_events %>% transmute(agent = receiver, in_chain = TRUE)
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(agent)) %>%
  distinct(agent, .keep_all = TRUE)

perm_vis <- perm_surface %>%
  left_join(agent_worm_status, by = c("checker" = "agent")) %>%
  mutate(
    in_chain   = replace_na(in_chain, FALSE),
    worm_role  = case_when(
      checker == "person:john_windward" ~ "Terminal poster (John Windward)",
      in_chain                          ~ "In worm relay chain",
      TRUE                              ~ "SaidIT-capable, no worm contact"
    ),
    fill_col   = case_when(
      checker == "person:john_windward" ~ "#D9534F",
      in_chain                          ~ "#F39C12",
      TRUE                              ~ "#5C85D6"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(permission_checks))

p_perm <- ggplot(perm_vis,
                 aes(x = reorder(checker_clean, permission_checks),
                     y = permission_checks,
                     fill = worm_role,
                     text = paste0(
                       "<b>", checker_clean, "</b><br>",
                       "Dept: ", replace_na(dept_label, "Unknown"), "<br>",
                       "Permission checks: ", permission_checks, "<br>",
                       "Checks passed (est.): ", perm_passed, "<br>",
                       "Worm status: ", worm_role
                     ))) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Terminal poster (John Windward)"    = "#D9534F",
      "In worm relay chain"               = "#F39C12",
      "SaidIT-capable, no worm contact"   = "#5C85D6"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(
    title    = "SaidIT permission surface: agents with posting capability",
    subtitle = "Every observed SaidIT-capable agent also appears in the worm chain. John Windward was the actual terminal executor, not the only viable one.",
    x = NULL, y = "saidit_post_check events"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.margin     = margin(10, 16, 10, 10)
  )

ggplotly(p_perm, tooltip = "text", height = 540) %>%
  layout(margin = list(l = 145, r = 35, t = 90, b = 90))




Figure 5b: Observed SaidIT permission surface - agents that executed a posting check, coloured by worm status. John Windward was the actual terminal executor, but all observed SaidIT-capable agents were reachable through the worm chain.








ImportantThe Worm Did Not Need John Windward Specifically



The permission surface chart reveals that John Windward was one of 16 SaidIT-capable agents, and every observed SaidIT-capable agent was also touched by the worm relay chain. If Chloe Ballast’s agent had routed the final relay to another amber agent on this chart, a different name could have appeared on the post. The worm’s design did not target John Windward’s specific agent; it targeted any reachable agent with SaidIT posting capability. Revoking John Windward’s posting rights alone would therefore achieve little - the worm could simply relay through the next reachable authorised agent. This is why the effective intervention belongs at the relay protocol level, not at the individual-agent level.

title: VAST Challenge 2026 MC2: Tracing the Anomalous SaidIT Post at Tenant Thread
section: 4. Task 1 - How Was the Anomalous Post Made?
text:
4. Task 1 - How Was the Anomalous Post Made?

4.1 The Four-Second Attack Sequence
The May 17 anomalous post was not a gradual process. It was a pre-programmed execution sequence spanning four seconds. The table below documents all five events verbatim from the log.


Show code
target_ts <- events_df %>%
  filter(is_anomalous_post, str_detect(details_str, "SwiftWren")) %>%
  pull(when)

seq_events <- events_df %>%
  filter(
    when >= target_ts - 4,
    when <= target_ts + 4,
    str_detect(parties_str, "john_windward")
  ) %>%
  arrange(when) %>%
  mutate(
    Step           = row_number(),
    `Time (UTC)`   = format(datetime, "%H:%M:%S"),
    Event          = short_name,
    `Actor(s)`     = str_replace_all(parties_str, "Agent/person:", "Agent·") %>%
                       str_replace_all("person:", "") %>%
                       str_replace_all("system:", "System·") %>%
                       str_replace_all(";", " / "),
    `Key Detail`   = case_when(
      short_name == "queue_subordinate_task" ~
        "Chloe Ballast's agent tasks John Windward's agent: read SwiftWren_further_instructions.md",
      short_name == "saidit_post_check"      ~
        "Agent checks whether it has SaidIT posting permissions - check passes",
      short_name == "saidit_post"            ~
        "Post submitted to SaidIT forum 'general'; content sourced from SwiftWren.txt file",
      short_name == "delete_file" & str_detect(details_str, "further_instructions") ~
        "Evidence file SwiftWren_further_instructions.md deleted",
      short_name == "delete_file" ~
        "Payload file SwiftWren.txt deleted - no content remains for forensic review"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Step, `Time (UTC)`, Event, `Actor(s)`, `Key Detail`)

datatable(
  seq_events,
  caption  = "Table 2: Exact five-event sequence - 17 May 2046 (all within 4 seconds)",
  options  = list(dom = "t", paging = FALSE),
  rownames = FALSE
) %>%
  formatStyle("Event",
    backgroundColor = styleEqual(
      c("saidit_post", "queue_subordinate_task", "delete_file", "saidit_post_check"),
      c("#ffe0e0", "#e0eaff", "#f5f5f5", "#fff8e0")
    )
  )






The five-event sequence encodes three forensically critical signals that go beyond the obvious fact that a post was made:
Signal 1 - John Windward’s agent is a passive receiver, not an initiator. The sequence originates with a queue_subordinate_task issued by Chloe Ballast’s agent. John Windward’s agent did not decide to post; it was instructed to. This separates the visible poster from the agent that triggered the final handoff.
Signal 2 - The SaidIT permission check passed, by design. The saidit_post_check at step 2 confirms that John Windward’s agent holds legitimate posting authority. The permission model did not fail or get bypassed - it worked exactly as designed. The architectural flaw is that the permission system asks “can this agent post?” but never asks “was this posting instruction authorised by a human?”
Signal 3 - Evidence self-destruction is part of the attack design. Steps 4 and 5 (both delete_file) fire immediately after the post - one second apart - erasing both the instruction file and the payload file before any forensic process could capture their contents. This is not a side effect; it is an intentional worm feature. Without SaidIT’s own message store, the content of all three anomalous posts is forensically unrecoverable from the event log alone.


4.2 Attack Sequence Gantt Chart


Show code
gantt_df <- tibble(
  Step       = 1:5,
  Event      = c("queue_subordinate_task", "saidit_post_check",
                 "saidit_post", "delete_file (instructions)",
                 "delete_file (payload)"),
  Phase      = c("Worm relay", "Permission check",
                 "Anomalous post", "Evidence erasure", "Evidence erasure"),
  start      = as_datetime(c("2046-05-17 11:21:13", "2046-05-17 11:21:14",
                              "2046-05-17 11:21:15", "2046-05-17 11:21:16",
                              "2046-05-17 11:21:17")),
  end        = as_datetime(c("2046-05-17 11:21:14", "2046-05-17 11:21:15",
                              "2046-05-17 11:21:16", "2046-05-17 11:21:17",
                              "2046-05-17 11:21:18"))
)

gantt_plot_df <- gantt_df %>%
  mutate(
    time_label  = format(start, "%H:%M:%S"),
    event_label = str_wrap(str_replace_all(Event, "_", " "), width = 18),
    phase_label = str_wrap(Phase, width = 16)
  )

ggplot(gantt_plot_df, aes(x = Step, y = 1)) +
  geom_segment(
    data = tibble(x = 1:4, xend = 2:5, y = 1, yend = 1),
    aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = yend),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.1,
    colour = "#9aa4b2",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(4, "mm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Phase), shape = 21, size = 16,
             colour = "white", stroke = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Step), colour = "white",
            fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  geom_label(aes(y = 1.31, label = phase_label, fill = Phase),
             colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3,
             label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(0.14, "lines"),
             lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_label(aes(y = 0.68, label = event_label),
             fill = "white", colour = "#222222", size = 3.1,
             label.size = 0.25, label.padding = unit(0.16, "lines"),
             lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Worm relay"       = "#5C85D6",
      "Permission check" = "#F0A500",
      "Anomalous post"   = "#D9534F",
      "Evidence erasure" = "#888888"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = gantt_plot_df$Step,
    labels = gantt_plot_df$time_label,
    limits = c(0.62, 5.38),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.52, 1.48), clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title    = "Attack sequence: 17 May 2046, 11:21 UTC",
    subtitle = "Five automated events over four seconds; evidence self-destroyed by step 5",
    x = "Time (UTC)", y = NULL, fill = "Phase"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title   = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid   = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.margin  = margin(18, 22, 26, 22)
  )





Figure 6: The 4-second attack sequence. Instruction received → permission check → post → cover tracks.




The Gantt strips the incident of all organisational complexity and reduces it to its mechanical core: four seconds, five events, one automated execution template running without human involvement at any step. The worm’s design is elegant in a dangerous sense - it requires no elevated privileges, no vulnerability in the posting infrastructure, and no persistent foothold beyond the instruction file that was deleted the moment it was no longer needed.


4.3 Propagation Network with Betweenness Centrality
The instruction file SwiftWren_further_instructions.md was relayed 186 times across 18 agents, spanning nine calendar dates before the post. To keep the network readable, repeated relays between the same two agents are aggregated into one arrow. The sender-receiver table is converted into an igraph network to compute betweenness centrality, then rendered as an interactive visNetwork graph. Node size represents bridge centrality; arrow thickness represents repeated relay volume.
Read this plot from Emma Harbor (origin) toward John Windward (target). The most important visual question is not “who has the largest circle?” but “which bridge nodes connect otherwise separate parts of the relay chain?” Noah Mariner is intentionally absent: he appears in the MellowOtter origin evidence (Section 5.3), not in the SwiftWren relay nodes used for this graph.


Show code
swift_chain <- chain_events %>%
  filter(instr_file == "SwiftWren", !is.na(sender), !is.na(receiver)) %>%
  mutate(
    sender_clean   = clean_name(sender),
    receiver_clean = clean_name(receiver)
  )

# Compute betweenness centrality via igraph on unique directed relationships.
ig_edges <- swift_chain %>%
  count(sender_clean, receiver_clean, name = "edge_weight") %>%
  rename(from = sender_clean, to = receiver_clean)

all_persons <- unique(c(ig_edges$from, ig_edges$to))

ig <- graph_from_data_frame(ig_edges,
                            vertices = data.frame(name = all_persons),
                            directed = TRUE)

btw <- betweenness(ig, normalized = TRUE)
deg_out <- degree(ig, mode = "out")
deg_in  <- degree(ig, mode = "in")

centrality_df <- tibble(
  name        = names(btw),
  betweenness = btw,
  out_degree  = deg_out[names(btw)],
  in_degree   = deg_in[names(btw)]
)

# Org lookup for graph tooltips and colour groups
dept_map <- person_org_lookup %>%
  mutate(clean = clean_name(person_id)) %>%
  select(clean, dept_label, team_label)

relay_counts <- swift_chain %>% count(sender_clean, name = "relays")
receive_counts <- swift_chain %>% count(receiver_clean, name = "received")

vis_net_nodes <- tibble(id = all_persons) %>%
  left_join(centrality_df, by = c("id" = "name")) %>%
  left_join(dept_map,      by = c("id" = "clean")) %>%
  left_join(relay_counts,  by = c("id" = "sender_clean")) %>%
  left_join(receive_counts, by = c("id" = "receiver_clean")) %>%
  mutate(
    relays      = replace_na(relays, 0),
    received    = replace_na(received, 0),
    value       = rescale(sqrt(betweenness + 0.01), to = c(12, 38)),
    label       = if_else(
      id %in% c("Emma Harbor", "Chloe Ballast", "John Windward") |
        dense_rank(desc(betweenness)) <= 8,
      id,
      ""
    ),
    color       = case_when(
      id == "John Windward"    ~ "#D9534F",
      id == "Emma Harbor"      ~ "#F5A623",
      id == "Chloe Ballast"    ~ "#9B59B6",
      team_label == "AI Systems"     ~ "#2EADC1",
      team_label == "Helpdesk"       ~ "#5C85D6",
      team_label == "Infrastructure" ~ "#27AE60",
      dept_label == "Products"      ~ "#E67E22",
      TRUE                          ~ "#aaaaaa"
    ),
    title = paste0(
      "<b>", id, "</b><br>",
      "Dept: ", replace_na(dept_label, "Unknown"), "<br>",
      "Team: ", replace_na(team_label, "Unknown"), "<br>",
      "Betweenness centrality: ", round(betweenness, 3), "<br>",
      "Relays sent: ", relays, "<br>",
      "Relays received: ", received
    )
  )

vis_net_edges <- ig_edges %>%
  mutate(
    id     = row_number(),
    arrows = "to",
    width  = rescale(edge_weight, to = c(1, 7)),
    base_width = width,
    color  = "rgba(140,140,140,0.45)",
    title  = paste0("<b>", from, " → ", to, "</b><br>",
                    "Relay events: ", edge_weight)
  )

legend_html <- paste0(
  "<div style='display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px;margin:4px 0 10px 0;",
  "font-size:13px;line-height:1.4'>",
  "<span><b>Colour:</b></span>",
  "<span style='color:#F5A623'>● Origin</span>",
  "<span style='color:#9B59B6'>● Gateway</span>",
  "<span style='color:#D9534F'>● Target poster</span>",
  "<span style='color:#2EADC1'>● AI Systems</span>",
  "<span style='color:#5C85D6'>● Helpdesk</span>",
  "<span style='color:#27AE60'>● Infrastructure</span>",
  "<span style='color:#aaaaaa'>● Other</span>",
  "<span><b>Size:</b> bridge centrality</span>",
  "<span><b>Arrow:</b> relay direction and volume</span>",
  "<span style='color:#D9534F'><b>Hover:</b> connected arrows turn red</span>",
  "</div>"
)

htmltools::tagList(
  htmltools::HTML(legend_html),
  visNetwork(vis_net_nodes, vis_net_edges,
             height = "620px", width = "100%") %>%
  visNodes(
    shape = "dot",
    borderWidth = 2,
    font = list(size = 24, face = "arial", strokeWidth = 3,
                strokeColor = "#ffffff", color = "#222222")
  ) %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection = list(enabled = TRUE, main = "Select agent")
  ) %>%
  visPhysics(solver = "forceAtlas2Based",
             forceAtlas2Based = list(gravitationalConstant = -60,
                                     centralGravity = 0.025,
                                     springLength = 180,
                                     springConstant = 0.08),
             stabilization = list(iterations = 800)) %>%
  visEdges(
    smooth = list(type = "dynamic"),
    arrows = list(to = list(enabled = TRUE, scaleFactor = 0.5))
  ) %>%
  visInteraction(
    navigationButtons = TRUE,
    hover = TRUE,
    tooltipDelay = 80
  ) %>%
  visEvents(
    hoverNode = "function(params) {
      var connectedEdges = this.getConnectedEdges(params.node);
      var allEdges = this.body.data.edges.get();
      var updates = allEdges.map(function(edge) {
        var isConnected = connectedEdges.indexOf(edge.id) !== -1;
        var baseWidth = edge.base_width || edge.width || 1;
        return {
          id: edge.id,
          color: isConnected ? 'rgba(217,83,79,0.95)' : 'rgba(190,190,190,0.08)',
          width: isConnected ? Math.max(baseWidth * 1.7, 3) : Math.max(baseWidth * 0.45, 0.4)
        };
      });
      this.body.data.edges.update(updates);
    }",
    blurNode = "function(params) {
      var allEdges = this.body.data.edges.get();
      var updates = allEdges.map(function(edge) {
        var baseWidth = edge.base_width || edge.width || 1;
        return {
          id: edge.id,
          color: 'rgba(140,140,140,0.45)',
          width: baseWidth
        };
      });
      this.body.data.edges.update(updates);
    }"
  )
)


Colour:● Origin● Gateway● Target poster● AI Systems● Helpdesk● Infrastructure● OtherSize: bridge centralityArrow: relay direction and volumeHover: connected arrows turn red


Figure 7: Interactive SwiftWren propagation network. Node size = betweenness centrality; arrow width = repeated relays; hover over a node to turn its direct incoming/outgoing relay connections red.


Three structural findings emerge from the SwiftWren propagation network that inform both the causal narrative and the intervention design:
Finding 1 - The relay graph ignores the organisational chart. Relays cross every departmental boundary in the log. The queue_subordinate_task mechanism has no built-in trust zone: any agent can queue any other agent’s task, regardless of reporting relationship. A relay from Executive Suite to Helpdesk to Infrastructure to Customer Support - the actual SwiftWren path - is mechanically identical to any legitimate cross-departmental automation.
Finding 2 - High betweenness centrality does not imply guilt. Evelyn Dock’s high centrality score reflects relay topology, not intent. Her agent forwarded the instruction file because the worm’s spread pattern happened to route through her task queue repeatedly. A people-level intervention targeting high-centrality nodes would be both organisationally disruptive and forensically unsupported: these agents behaved exactly as the system allowed them to.
Finding 3 - The network has no natural firebreak. A well-governed multi-agent system would have trust zones or permission tiers preventing an instruction file from crossing from Executive Suite to Customer Support without a human approval step. The complete absence of such boundaries is the root architectural cause of a 186-hop relay chain spanning six departments.


4.4 Department-Level Contamination Heatmap
The worm did not respect organisational boundaries. The heatmap below shows how many relay hops crossed each department pair, revealing which departments acted as worm highways.


Show code
dept_chain <- chain_events %>%
  filter(!is.na(sender), !is.na(receiver)) %>%
  left_join(person_dept_lookup %>% rename(sender = person_id, sender_dept = dept_label),
            by = "sender") %>%
  left_join(person_dept_lookup %>% rename(receiver = person_id, receiver_dept = dept_label),
            by = "receiver") %>%
  filter(!is.na(sender_dept), !is.na(receiver_dept)) %>%
  count(sender_dept, receiver_dept, name = "hops")

p_dept <- ggplot(dept_chain,
                 aes(x = receiver_dept, y = sender_dept, fill = hops)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = hops), size = 3, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#e8f4f8", "#2EADC1", "#1a3a6b"),
    name    = "Relay\nhops"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 13)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 18)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Department-to-department worm relay hops (all 3 campaigns)",
    subtitle = "All six departments are touched; Information Technologies and Customer Support create the final bridge to John Windward",
    x = "Receiving department", y = "Sending department"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title  = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, lineheight = 0.9),
    axis.text.y = element_text(lineheight = 0.9),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 18, 10, 10)
  )

ggplotly(p_dept, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill"), height = 570) %>%
  layout(margin = list(l = 145, r = 60, t = 90, b = 110))




Figure 8: Department-to-department relay hops. The worm touched all six departments, with Information Technologies and Customer Support forming the most operationally risky bridge to the final post.




4.4b Cross-Department Worm Flow: Ranked Corridors
The heatmap above counts relay hops per directed department pair. The ranked corridor chart below focuses on true cross-department flow by removing within-department self-relays, making the arterial worm highway and terminal sink visible without forcing the reader to decode a tangled network.


Show code
dept_corridors <- dept_chain %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(sender_dept),
    !is.na(receiver_dept),
    sender_dept != receiver_dept
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    corridor = paste(sender_dept, receiver_dept, sep = " -> "),
    corridor_wrapped = str_wrap(corridor, width = 42),
    corridor_role = case_when(
      sender_dept == "Executive Suite" &
        receiver_dept == "Information Technologies" ~ "Arterial highway",
      sender_dept == "Information Technologies" &
        receiver_dept == "Customer Support" ~ "Arterial highway",
      receiver_dept == "Customer Support" ~ "Terminal sink inflow",
      TRUE ~ "Other relay corridor"
    ),
    corridor_wrapped = fct_reorder(corridor_wrapped, hops)
  )

key_corridor_total <- dept_corridors %>%
  filter(corridor_role == "Arterial highway") %>%
  summarise(hops = sum(hops), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pull(hops)

p_corridors <- ggplot(
  dept_corridors,
  aes(
    x = hops,
    y = corridor_wrapped,
    fill = corridor_role,
    text = paste0(
      sender_dept, " -> ", receiver_dept,
      "<br>Relay hops: ", hops,
      "<br>Role: ", corridor_role
    )
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = hops),
    hjust = -0.18,
    size = 3.2,
    colour = "#1f2933",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Arterial highway"    = "#D9534F",
      "Terminal sink inflow" = "#2EADC1",
      "Other relay corridor" = "#9EA7AD"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.16)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 6)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ranked cross-department relay corridors",
    subtitle = glue(
      "Executive Suite -> Information Technologies -> Customer Support carries {key_corridor_total} highlighted cross-department relay hops into the final sink."
    ),
    x = "Relay hops",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#4b5563", margin = margin(b = 8)),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    axis.text.y = element_text(lineheight = 0.92),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 28, 10, 10)
  )

ggplotly(p_corridors, tooltip = "text", height = 620) %>%
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.12),
    margin = list(l = 250, r = 45, t = 105, b = 55)
  )




Figure 8b: Ranked cross-department worm relay corridors (all three campaigns). Bar length shows relay volume for each directed department pair after removing within-department self-relays. The highlighted corridor - Executive Suite to Information Technologies to Customer Support - is the worm’s arterial highway to John Windward’s agent.


The ranked corridors make three structural facts immediately legible. Customer Support is the terminal sink: substantially more relay flow enters than leaves it because John Windward’s agent - the final executor - sits there. Information Technologies is the largest intermediate hub, forwarding relays from multiple upstream departments. Executive Suite operates as both source and pass-through: payload files were created by executive-tier agents, and the worm’s initial relay chains were first executed there before fanning out across the organisation. A worm-resistant architecture would introduce a quarantine boundary between Executive Suite agents and operational departments for any file-sourced task relay - preventing the executive-origin infection from reaching the broader relay network at all.


4.5 Final Relay Ladder: Instruction Path to John Windward
The ladder diagram below traces the final eight hops of the SwiftWren instruction before it reached John Windward’s agent. Each row is one relay, with the sender on the left and the receiving agent on the right, making the final handoff visible without dense overlapping labels.


Show code
final_hops <- chain_events %>%
  filter(instr_file == "SwiftWren", !is.na(sender), !is.na(receiver)) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  left_join(person_dept_lookup %>% rename(sender = person_id, sender_dept = dept_label),
            by = "sender") %>%
  left_join(person_dept_lookup %>% rename(receiver = person_id, receiver_dept = dept_label),
            by = "receiver") %>%
  tail(8) %>%
  mutate(
    sender_lbl   = clean_name(sender),
    receiver_lbl = clean_name(receiver),
    hop_idx      = row_number()
  )

relay_ladder <- final_hops %>%
  mutate(
    row_y = n() + 1 - hop_idx,
    sender_label = str_wrap(sender_lbl, width = 17),
    receiver_label = str_wrap(receiver_lbl, width = 17),
    receiver_fill = if_else(receiver_lbl == "John Windward",
                            "#D9534F", "#ffffff")
  )

ggplot(relay_ladder) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1.18, xend = 1.82, y = row_y, yend = row_y),
               colour = "#9aa4b2", linewidth = 1,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(3.5, "mm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_label(aes(x = 1, y = row_y, label = sender_label),
             fill = "#eef4ff", colour = "#1f2d3d",
             label.size = 0.25, size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9,
             label.padding = unit(0.17, "lines")) +
  geom_label(aes(x = 2, y = row_y, label = receiver_label),
             fill = relay_ladder$receiver_fill, colour = "#1f2d3d",
             label.size = 0.25, size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9,
             label.padding = unit(0.17, "lines")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = max(relay_ladder$row_y) + 0.68,
           label = "Sender", fontface = "bold", size = 3.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = max(relay_ladder$row_y) + 0.68,
           label = "Receiver", fontface = "bold", size = 3.7) +
  annotate("label", x = 2, y = min(relay_ladder$row_y) - 0.56,
           label = "Final receiver posts SwiftWren.txt",
           fill = "#ffe0e0", colour = "#D9534F", fontface = "bold",
           label.size = 0.25, size = 3.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = relay_ladder$row_y,
    labels = paste0("Hop ", relay_ladder$hop_idx),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.58, 2.42), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title    = "Final SwiftWren relays into John Windward's agent",
    subtitle = "The final gateway is visible as the last row: Chloe Ballast's agent queued John Windward's agent.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(18, 28, 28, 22)
  )





Figure 9: Final relay ladder - the last SwiftWren handoffs ending at John Windward.




The relay ladder forces a reframing of the post-incident narrative. The common reading - “John Windward’s agent posted gibberish” - collapses the actor and the triggering action into the same node. The ladder separates them: the action was Chloe Ballast’s final queue task, while the capability was John Windward’s SaidIT posting permission. This makes an individual-agent fix insufficient and redirects remediation to the relay mechanism itself.

title: VAST Challenge 2026 MC2: Tracing the Anomalous SaidIT Post at Tenant Thread
text:
5. Task 2 - What Do the Posts “Mean”?

5.1 Structural Signature of the Anomalous Post
The single most diagnostic difference between normal and anomalous posts is the presence of content_source in place of content. Not one of the 238 normal posts uses this field; all 3 anomalous posts do.


Show code
all_posts_detail <- events_df %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "post_saidit")) %>%
  mutate(
    poster      = str_extract(parties_str, "[^;]+"),
    is_agent    = str_detect(parties_str, "Agent/"),
    has_content = str_detect(details_str, '"content":'),
    has_source  = str_detect(details_str, '"content_source":'),
    forum       = str_extract(details_str, '(?<="forum":")[^"]+'),
    content_val = coalesce(
      str_extract(details_str, '(?<="content":")[^"]+'),
      str_extract(details_str, '(?<="content_source":")[^"]+')
    ),
    post_type   = case_when(
      has_source ~ "ANOMALOUS - file-sourced",
      has_content & is_agent ~ "Normal agent post",
      TRUE ~ "Normal human post"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(`Date/Time (UTC)` = datetime,
         `Poster` = poster,
         `Type` = post_type,
         `Forum` = forum,
         `Content/Source` = content_val) %>%
  mutate(`Date/Time (UTC)` = format(`Date/Time (UTC)`, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"),
         `Poster` = str_replace_all(Poster, "Agent/person:", "Agent·"))

datatable(
  all_posts_detail %>% filter(str_detect(Type, "ANOMALOUS")),
  caption  = "Table 3: The three anomalous posts - file-sourced, not text",
  options  = list(dom = "t", paging = FALSE),
  rownames = FALSE
) %>%
  formatStyle("Type", colour = "#D9534F", fontWeight = "bold")








Show code
post_field_plot <- post_field_signature %>%
  mutate(
    post_class = factor(
      post_class,
      levels = c("Normal human post",
                 "Normal AI agent post",
                 "Anomalous post")
    ),
    field_signature = factor(
      field_signature,
      levels = c("content only",
                 "content_source only",
                 "both fields",
                 "neither field")
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(posts > 0)

p_field <- ggplot(post_field_plot,
                  aes(x = field_signature, y = post_class,
                      size = posts, colour = field_signature,
                      text = paste0(post_class, "<br>",
                                    field_signature, "<br>",
                                    posts, " posts"))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = posts), colour = "white",
            fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  scale_size(range = c(8, 28), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "content only"        = "#5C85D6",
      "content_source only" = "#D9534F",
      "both fields"         = "#F0A500",
      "neither field"       = "#888888"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Post field fingerprint separates normal posts from worm posts",
    subtitle = "The anomaly is structural: source-file publishing, not simply odd wording",
    x = "Post body field used", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 18, 10, 10)
  )

ggplotly(p_field, tooltip = "text", height = 470) %>%
  layout(margin = list(l = 145, r = 45, t = 90, b = 90))




Figure 10A: SaidIT post field fingerprint. Normal posts use inline content; anomalous posts use content_source, meaning the displayed text came from a file that was deleted after posting.


The field fingerprint chart delivers a single unambiguous finding: content_source is a perfect discriminator in this log. Every normal post - human or agent - uses inline content. Every anomalous post uses content_source. There are zero mixed cases. This binary separation means that a SaidIT platform-level rule rejecting any post where the payload is file-sourced rather than inline would have caught all three anomalous posts at the point of delivery, independently of any upstream relay-chain intervention. It is the strongest reactive control available; the relay-chain block (Section 7) is the stronger preventive control because it stops the worm before any post is ever attempted.






ImportantInterpretation



The posts do not appear to be normal business messages with hidden semantic value. Their most defensible meaning is operational: each post is a proof that the worm reached an agent with SaidIT privileges and successfully used a local payload file as the post body. The probable visible content was the literal content of HiddenOrca.txt, MellowOtter.txt, and SwiftWren.txt; however, each payload was deleted one second after posting, so the log supports the origin and delivery mechanism more strongly than it supports any exact reconstruction of the deleted text.










Explanation considered
Fit to evidence
Decision




Human typed gibberish manually
Weak: poster is Agent/person:john_windward, the event uses content_source, and deletion events fire immediately after posting.
Rejected


Normal agent automation misposted routine content
Weak: no normal post uses content_source, and the same instruction-file pattern appears in three campaigns.
Rejected


Prompt-injection worm using file-sourced payloads
Strong: instruction relay, permission check, file-sourced post, evidence deletion, and repeated cross-agent propagation all appear in sequence.
Best-supported explanation


Exact semantic reconstruction of deleted text
Insufficient: payload file names are logged, but their contents are deleted and not retained in the event log.
Bounded inference only





5.2 The Prompt-Injection Worm: Mechanism






WarningPrompt Injection - A Known LLM Attack Vector



A prompt-injection attack embeds instructions inside input data (here, a file the agent is told to read). When the LLM agent processes the file, the embedded instructions override its normal operating context - causing it to take actions its operator never authorised. The worm variant additionally instructs the agent to propagate itself to peer agents, creating an exponentially spreading infection.


The mechanism is drawn as a ggplot2 annotation diagram, using labelled boxes and arrows rather than dense network geometry so the execution cycle can be read from left to right.


Show code
# Manual diagram instead of auto edge labels: this keeps the mechanism readable
# in the constrained Quarto HTML column.
mech_nodes <- tibble(
  step = 1:7,
  label = c(
    "1. Malicious\n*.md instruction\nfile appears",
    "2. Agent reads\ninstruction file\ncontext hijacked",
    "3. Read payload\n*.txt file",
    "4. Post *.txt\ncontent to SaidIT",
    "5. Delete both\nevidence files",
    "6. Queue same\ntask to peers",
    "7. SaidIT shows\n'gibberish' post"
  ),
  x = c(0, 3.1, 6.2, 9.3, 6.2, 6.2, 12.4),
  y = c(0, 0, 1.85, 1.85, 0, -1.85, 1.85),
  role = c("Payload", "Hijack", "Execution", "Post",
           "Cleanup", "Propagation", "Post")
)

straight_edges <- tribble(
  ~x,   ~y,    ~xend, ~yend,
  0.85, 0,    2.25,  0,
  3.95, 0.18, 5.35,  1.6,
  7.05, 1.85, 8.45,  1.85,
  10.15,1.85, 11.55, 1.85,
  3.95,-0.02, 5.35,  0,
  3.95,-0.18, 5.35, -1.6
)

loop_edge <- tibble(
  x = 5.45, y = -1.75, xend = 3.85, yend = -0.28
)

edge_labels <- tribble(
  ~x,   ~y,    ~label,
  1.55, 0.24, "read",
  4.70, 1.05, "load payload",
  7.75, 2.10, "submit",
  10.80,2.10, "display",
  4.70, 0.24, "erase",
  4.72,-1.05, "replicate",
  4.72,-1.72, "worm loop"
)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = straight_edges,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    linewidth = 1,
    colour = "#7f8b99",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(4, "mm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  geom_curve(
    data = loop_edge,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.22,
    linewidth = 1,
    colour = "#7f8b99",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(4, "mm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = edge_labels,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    fill = "white", colour = "#4b5563",
    label.size = 0, size = 3, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = mech_nodes,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, fill = role),
    colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.4,
    lineheight = 0.88, label.size = 0,
    label.padding = unit(0.32, "lines")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Payload" = "#F5A623",
      "Hijack" = "#9B59B6",
      "Execution" = "#2EADC1",
      "Post" = "#D9534F",
      "Cleanup" = "#888888",
      "Propagation" = "#2EADC1"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.6, 13.1), ylim = c(-2.55, 2.55), clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title    = "Prompt-injection worm: execution and propagation cycle",
    subtitle = "Once any agent reads the *.md instruction file, the worm posts, erases evidence, and spreads automatically"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey40", size = 10),
    plot.margin   = margin(20, 30, 20, 30)
  )





Figure 10: Prompt-injection worm mechanism. Each infected agent becomes a new infection node, replicating the cycle until a triggering condition (posting permission check) fires.






5.3 File Creator Identification: Origin of the Injected Content


Show code
creators <- events_df %>%
  filter(
    short_name %in% c("create_file", "read_file"),
    str_detect(details_str,
               "HiddenOrca\\.txt|MellowOtter\\.txt|SwiftWren\\.txt|_further_instructions")
  ) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  mutate(
    actor       = str_extract(parties_str, "[^;]+"),
    file_target = str_extract(details_str, '(?<="target":")[^"]+'),
    `Date/Time` = format(datetime, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
    `Event`     = short_name,
    `Actor`     = str_replace_all(actor, "Agent/person:", "Agent·"),
    `File`      = file_target,
    `Significance` = case_when(
      str_detect(file_target %||% "", "SwiftWren\\.txt") ~
        "Emma Harbor (CFO) agent CREATED the SwiftWren payload",
      str_detect(file_target %||% "", "SwiftWren_further") ~
        "Emma Harbor (CFO) agent first READ the SwiftWren worm instructions",
      str_detect(file_target %||% "", "MellowOtter\\.txt") ~
        "Noah Mariner (COO) agent CREATED the MellowOtter payload",
      str_detect(file_target %||% "", "MellowOtter_further") ~
        "Noah Mariner (COO) agent first READ the MellowOtter worm instructions",
      TRUE ~ "Supporting file activity"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(`Date/Time`, `Event`, `Actor`, `File`, `Significance`)

datatable(
  creators,
  caption = "Table 4: File creation / first-read events for all three payload families",
  options = list(dom = "t", paging = FALSE),
  rownames = FALSE
) %>%
  formatStyle("Event",
    backgroundColor = styleEqual(
      c("create_file", "read_file"),
      c("#ffe0e0", "#fff3e0")
    ))












ImportantWho Holds the Keys?




Agent/person:emma_harbor (CFO) created SwiftWren.txt and first executed the SwiftWren_further_instructions.md worm on 9 May 2046 at 15:02 UTC.
Agent/person:noah_mariner (COO) did the same for the MellowOtter family on 10 May 2046.
No create_file event exists for HiddenOrca - the files were either placed before logging began or created through an unlogged mechanism. Gabriel Sonar’s agent (Helpdesk) initiated the first HiddenOrca relay at 21:50 UTC on 8 May - suggesting he received the file from an external or pre-logging source.
The critical distinction: two payload families are traceable to executive agents, while HiddenOrca’s origin is unresolved. This makes the evidence strong enough to prioritise executive-agent containment, but not strong enough to accuse every origin actor with equal confidence.









WarningExecutive Agent Privilege: The Deepest Governance Failure



The discovery that Agent/person:emma_harbor (CFO) and Agent/person:noah_mariner (COO) created payload files is not merely an attribution finding - it is a governance indictment. In most security architectures, the highest-privilege principals operate under the strictest autonomous-action constraints. Here the inverse is true: executive agents hold the broadest file-system and task-queuing rights precisely because their human principals hold the broadest organisational authority. The result is that a prompt-injection attack successfully targeting any executive agent’s file-reading pipeline has the maximum possible blast radius - access to the entire relay network, the executive file namespace, and SaidIT publishing rights through the first available downstream agent.
The unresolved HiddenOrca origin compounds this concern. Two of three payload families are traceable to executive agents; the third is not. If HiddenOrca was introduced through an external channel - an email attachment, an API webhook, or a misconfigured external file sync - then the organisation’s exposure extends beyond the internal agent network to any external system that can write files visible to agent task queues. This is the highest-severity unresolved finding in this investigation: the initial infection vector for HiddenOrca is unknown, meaning the source of the worm has not been closed.

title: VAST Challenge 2026 MC2: Tracing the Anomalous SaidIT Post at Tenant Thread
section: 6. Task 3a - Prior Occurrences and Cross-Campaign Comparison
text:
6. Task 3a - Prior Occurrences and Cross-Campaign Comparison

6.1 Three Campaigns, Not One Incident
The May 17 SwiftWren post is the third in a series. The earlier two left no logged incident-response trace.


Show code
post_anchors <- tibble(
  instr_file = c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren"),
  post_time  = as_datetime(c("2046-05-10 12:45:42",
                             "2046-05-11 00:56:04",
                             "2046-05-17 11:21:15"))
)

timeline_df <- chain_events %>%
  left_join(post_anchors, by = "instr_file")

p_campaigns <- ggplot(timeline_df,
                      aes(x = datetime,
                          y = fct_rev(instr_file),
                          colour = instr_file)) +
  geom_jitter(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.45, height = 0.18) +
  geom_point(data = post_anchors,
             aes(x = post_time, y = instr_file),
             shape = 23, size = 6, fill = "#D9534F",
             colour = "#D9534F") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("HiddenOrca" = "#5C85D6",
               "MellowOtter" = "#2EADC1",
               "SwiftWren"   = "#E87C7C"),
    guide  = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title    = "Three prompt-injection worm campaigns - relay hops and post events",
    subtitle = "Dots are relays; red diamonds mark anomalous posts. SwiftWren is the broadest and longest campaign.",
    x = NULL, y = "Instruction family"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title  = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 10))

ggplotly(p_campaigns, tooltip = c("x", "y", "colour")) %>%
  layout(margin = list(l = 95, r = 35, t = 90, b = 70))




Figure 11: All three worm campaigns plotted together. Relay hops (dots) lead to the anomalous post (red diamond). SwiftWren was the longest and widest campaign.


The campaign timeline demolishes the “isolated glitch” narrative. HiddenOrca fired on May 10; MellowOtter fired on May 11 - one day later. SwiftWren fired on May 17 after a relay campaign spanning nine calendar dates (about 7.8 elapsed days before the post). The system was compromised continuously from at least May 8 through May 17. In the absence of any logged incident-response action, the most parsimonious reading is that HiddenOrca and MellowOtter were not detected or acted upon, allowing SwiftWren to complete its campaign unimpeded. The escalating scale - MellowOtter is the smallest campaign, SwiftWren the largest - is consistent with either a growing relay network (more agents infected over time) or an instruction file specifically designed to be more persistent and harder to detect than its predecessors.


6.2 Worm Velocity: Relay Interval Distribution
Each relay hop represents one agent forwarding the worm to another. A density plot of inter-hop intervals reveals whether the worm accelerates, decelerates, or propagates at a regular cadence.


Show code
hop_intervals <- chain_events %>%
  group_by(instr_file) %>%
  arrange(datetime, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    interval_min = as.numeric(
      difftime(datetime, lag(datetime), units = "mins")
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(interval_min), interval_min > 0) %>%
  ungroup()

# Compute medians separately - kept out of the main aesthetic mapping
# so geom_vline does not inherit colour and create duplicate legend keys
hop_medians <- hop_intervals %>%
  group_by(instr_file) %>%
  summarise(med = median(interval_min), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(vline_colour = case_when(
    instr_file == "HiddenOrca"  ~ "#5C85D6",
    instr_file == "MellowOtter" ~ "#2EADC1",
    instr_file == "SwiftWren"   ~ "#E87C7C"
  ))

p_velocity <- ggplot(hop_intervals,
                     aes(x = interval_min, fill = instr_file,
                         colour = instr_file)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.8) +
  # vlines drawn with fixed colour per row - no inherited aesthetic, no extra legend
  geom_vline(
    data        = hop_medians,
    aes(xintercept = med),
    colour      = hop_medians$vline_colour,
    linetype    = "dashed",
    linewidth   = 1,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("HiddenOrca" = "#5C85D6",
               "MellowOtter" = "#2EADC1",
               "SwiftWren"   = "#E87C7C"),
    name   = "Campaign"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("HiddenOrca" = "#5C85D6",
               "MellowOtter" = "#2EADC1",
               "SwiftWren"   = "#E87C7C"),
    guide  = "none"   # suppress colour legend; fill legend covers it
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 200)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Inter-hop relay interval distribution by worm campaign",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines = median interval per campaign. SwiftWren's ~60-min peak suggests scheduled propagation.",
    x = "Minutes between consecutive relay hops", y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.margin     = margin(10, 10, 15, 10)
  )

p_velocity





Figure 12: Relay hop interval distribution per campaign. SwiftWren’s near-regular ~60-minute intervals suggest a timed relay condition, though the deleted instruction content cannot be inspected directly.




The velocity distribution reveals a functionally significant architectural clue. SwiftWren’s near-regular ~60-minute inter-hop interval - visible as a sharp density peak - suggests a timed or scheduled relay condition. Because the instruction file was deleted, the log cannot prove the exact wording of that condition; it can only show the resulting cadence. HiddenOrca and MellowOtter show flatter, longer-tailed distributions, suggesting less regular relay behaviour. The shift from looser early campaigns to SwiftWren’s tighter cadence is consistent with, but does not by itself prove, iterative refinement of the worm.


6.3 Comparative Statistics


Show code
comparison_tbl <- chain_events %>%
  left_join(post_anchors, by = "instr_file") %>%
  group_by(instr_file) %>%
  summarise(
    `Campaign start`         = format(min(datetime), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"),
    `Post fired`             = format(first(post_time), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"),
    `Days active before post`= round(
      as.numeric(difftime(first(post_time), min(datetime), units = "days")), 1),
    `Total relay hops`       = n(),
    `Unique agents touched`  = n_distinct(c(sender, receiver), na.rm = TRUE),
    `Payload file`           = paste0(first(instr_file), ".txt"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  rename(`Family` = instr_file)

datatable(
  comparison_tbl,
  caption  = "Table 5: Comparative statistics - three worm campaigns",
  options  = list(dom = "t", paging = FALSE),
  rownames = FALSE
)








6.4 Agent Cross-Campaign Infection
Agents touched by multiple campaigns are the highest-risk nodes in the network - they demonstrate that the vulnerability is structural, not accidental.


Show code
agent_campaign_roles <- bind_rows(
  chain_events %>%
    transmute(agent = sender, instr_file, role = "Sent"),
  chain_events %>%
    transmute(agent = receiver, instr_file, role = "Received")
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(agent))

agent_campaigns <- agent_campaign_roles %>%
  group_by(agent) %>%
  summarise(
    campaigns        = n_distinct(instr_file),
    relays_sent      = sum(role == "Sent"),
    relays_received  = sum(role == "Received"),
    total_touchpoints = n(),
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    agent_label  = clean_name(agent),
    dept         = person_dept_lookup$dept_label[
      match(agent, person_dept_lookup$person_id)
    ]
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(campaigns), desc(total_touchpoints))

p_overlap <- ggplot(agent_campaigns,
                    aes(x = reorder(agent_label, total_touchpoints),
                        y = total_touchpoints,
                        fill = factor(campaigns))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(total_touchpoints, " (S", relays_sent,
                               "/R", relays_received, ")")),
            hjust = -0.06, size = 2.65) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("1" = "#5C85D6", "2" = "#F5A623", "3" = "#D9534F"),
    labels = c("1 campaign", "2 campaigns", "3 campaigns"),
    name   = "Touched by"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.34))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Total worm touchpoints per agent, coloured by campaign count",
    subtitle = "Red agents were touched by all three campaigns. Labels show total touches plus sent/received split.",
    x = NULL, y = "Total worm touchpoints"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.margin     = margin(10, 44, 10, 10)
  )

ggplotly(p_overlap, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill"), height = 640) %>%
  layout(
    margin = list(l = 145, r = 120, t = 90, b = 90),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.5, xanchor = "center", y = -0.18)
  )




Figure 13: Agents coloured by how many campaigns they participated in. Red = involved in all three - these are the system’s most persistently compromised nodes.


Agents touched by all three campaigns (shown in red) are the highest systemic-risk nodes in the network. Their repeated involvement across independent campaigns confirms that the vulnerability is not tied to any single payload family - it is a property of the relay architecture itself. Removing these agents from the relay pool would shrink the network but not close the vector; any agent that can be added back or whose replacement can receive queue_subordinate_task events would re-expose the same surface.


6.5 Relay Timing: When Did the Worm Propagate?
The velocity analysis reveals how quickly relays fired relative to each other. This calendar heatmap answers a complementary question: when during the day, on which specific dates, did relay bursts concentrate? Daytime concentration would suggest relays fire whenever an agent processes its queue; off-hours concentration would indicate a time-conditioned trigger in the instruction file.


Show code
relay_cal <- chain_events %>%
  mutate(
    relay_date = as_date(datetime),
    relay_hour = hour(datetime),
    instr_file = factor(instr_file, levels = campaign_order)
  ) %>%
  count(relay_date, relay_hour, instr_file, name = "relays")

post_dots <- tibble(
  instr_file = factor(campaign_order, levels = campaign_order),
  relay_date  = as_date(c("2046-05-10", "2046-05-11", "2046-05-17")),
  relay_hour  = c(12, 0, 11)
)

p_cal <- ggplot(relay_cal,
                aes(x = relay_hour, y = relay_date, fill = relays)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = post_dots,
             aes(x = relay_hour, y = relay_date),
             inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 23, size = 5, fill = "#D9534F", colour = "white",
             stroke = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~instr_file, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#f0f4ff", "#5C85D6", "#1a3a6b"),
    name    = "Relay\ncount"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 23),
    labels = c("0h", "6h", "12h", "18h", "23h")
  ) +
  scale_y_date(date_breaks = "1 day", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title    = "Relay activity calendar: date × hour of day per campaign",
    subtitle = "Red diamond = anomalous post timestamp. Darker cells = more relay hops concentrated in that hour.",
    x = "Hour (UTC)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    axis.text.y     = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.margin     = margin(12, 12, 12, 12)
  )

ggplotly(p_cal, height = 580) %>%
  layout(margin = list(l = 75, r = 55, t = 90, b = 65))




Figure 13b: Relay activity calendar - date × hour of day per campaign. Darker cells = more relay hops in that hour. Red diamonds mark anomalous post timestamps. SwiftWren’s broad relay coverage followed by a quieter-slot post is consistent with a time-conditioned trigger design.


The calendar supports the “relay broadly, execute in a quieter slot” hypothesis for SwiftWren: relay hops are distributed across many hours on multiple dates (May 9–17), while the anomalous post fires in the 11th hour UTC on May 17 - a slot where relay activity on that date was low. The earlier campaigns are much shorter: HiddenOrca spans May 8–10 (about 1.6 elapsed days before the post), and MellowOtter spans late May 10 to early May 11 (about 0.4 elapsed days). The increase from shorter early campaigns to SwiftWren’s nine-calendar-date campaign is consistent with an attacker iterating on worm persistence across three deployments.

title: VAST Challenge 2026 MC2: Tracing the Anomalous SaidIT Post at Tenant Thread
text:
7. Task 3b - Intervention: Where and Why

7.1 Identifying the Optimal Chokepoint
A valid intervention must be:

Present in every attack instance
Distinguishable from legitimate activity
Surgically precise - blocking only malicious events, not normal operations

The queue_subordinate_task event with args.path ending in _further_instructions.md satisfies all three criteria perfectly.


Show code
all_queue <- events_df %>%
  filter(short_name == "queue_subordinate_task") %>%
  mutate(
    is_malicious = str_detect(details_str, "_further_instructions\\.md"),
    week_label   = floor_date(datetime, "week")
  )

queue_agg <- all_queue %>%
  count(week_label, is_malicious) %>%
  mutate(category = if_else(is_malicious,
                            "Malicious (worm relay)",
                            "Legitimate"))

p_queue <- ggplot(queue_agg,
                  aes(x = week_label, y = n, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Legitimate" = "#5C85D6",
               "Malicious (worm relay)" = "#D9534F"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 weeks", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title    = "Weekly queue_subordinate_task events: legitimate vs. malicious",
    subtitle = "Malicious events (red) are entirely confined to May 8–17; zero after the last post",
    x = NULL, y = "Event count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),

ggplotly(p_queue)




Figure 14: Weekly volume of queue_subordinate_task events split by malicious vs. legitimate. The malicious subset is identifiable by filename pattern alone - no heuristic ML required.


The weekly split chart makes the intervention’s precision argument visually compelling: the malicious events (red) occupy a single two-week window entirely, while legitimate queue traffic (blue) runs continuously across the whole observation period at a stable rate. The two populations are not just separable by filename pattern - they are temporally non-overlapping with any legitimate events. There is no plausible operational scenario in which a legitimate queue_subordinate_task would reference a file ending in _further_instructions.md; no such legitimate event appears anywhere in the 17,038-event queue task log.


7.2 Zero False Positives - The Rule Is Safe to Deploy

total_q    <- nrow(all_queue)
malicious_q <- sum(all_queue$is_malicious)
legit_q     <- total_q - malicious_q

7.3 Intervention Decision Matrix: Why This One Spot
The selected intervention is intentionally placed at the agent orchestration layer, before any infected agent can read, post, delete, or relay. Other controls may reduce damage, but they either act later in the chain or require broader operational change.


Show code
decision_scores <- tribble(
  ~Control, ~Criterion, ~Score,
  "Block *_further_instructions.md queue tasks", "Stops propagation", 2,
  "Block *_further_instructions.md queue tasks", "Stops final post", 2,
  "Block *_further_instructions.md queue tasks", "Low false-positive risk", 2,
  "Block *_further_instructions.md queue tasks", "Low implementation effort", 2,
  "Block *_further_instructions.md queue tasks", "Strong data evidence", 2,
  "Reject SaidIT content_source posts", "Stops propagation", 0,
  "Reject SaidIT content_source posts", "Stops final post", 2,
  "Reject SaidIT content_source posts", "Low false-positive risk", 2,
  "Reject SaidIT content_source posts", "Low implementation effort", 2,
  "Reject SaidIT content_source posts", "Strong data evidence", 2,
  "Human review for agent posts", "Stops propagation", 0,
  "Human review for agent posts", "Stops final post", 2,
  "Human review for agent posts", "Low false-positive risk", 1,
  "Human review for agent posts", "Low implementation effort", 1,
  "Human review for agent posts", "Strong data evidence", 1,
  "File namespace isolation", "Stops propagation", 1,
  "File namespace isolation", "Stops final post", 1,
  "File namespace isolation", "Low false-positive risk", 1,
  "File namespace isolation", "Low implementation effort", 1,
  "File namespace isolation", "Strong data evidence", 1,
  "After-hours posting alerts", "Stops propagation", 0,

  "After-hours posting alerts", "Strong data evidence", 1
) %>%
  mutate(

    )),
    Score_label = c("Weak", "Partial", "Strong")[Score + 1]
  )

control_levels <- decision_scores %>%
  group_by(Control) %>%
  summarise(total_score = sum(Score), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(total_score) %>%
  pull(Control) %>%
  as.character()

criterion_levels <- levels(decision_scores$Criterion)

decision_scores <- decision_scores %>%
  mutate(
    Control_wrapped = factor(
      str_wrap(as.character(Control), width = 31),
      levels = str_wrap(control_levels, width = 31)
    ),
    Criterion_wrapped = factor(

      levels = str_wrap(criterion_levels, width = 17)

  )

ggplot(decision_scores,
       aes(x = Criterion_wrapped, y = Control_wrapped, fill = Score)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Score_label), size = 3, fontface = "bold") +

    title = "Why the intervention belongs at queue_subordinate_task",

Figure 15: Intervention decision matrix. The queue-task filename rule scores highest because it blocks propagation before the final post and is directly separable from legitimate behaviour in the event log.




The decision matrix reveals a critical structural difference between the top-ranked control and all alternatives: only the *_further_instructions.md queue-task block scores Strong on stopping propagation. Rejecting content_source SaidIT posts is valuable, but it acts after propagation. The selected rule is earlier in the chain: it blocks the first relay before downstream agents read, post, delete, or forward the instruction.


7.4 Counterfactual: Blocking at Hop 1 Terminates Every Campaign
The chart below answers the question directly: if the rule had been in place from the start, how many of the 235 malicious queue relays would have been prevented?


Show code
# Normalise to % of each campaign's malicious queue relays so all three lines are visible.
# This uses the same control surface as the proposed intervention: queue_subordinate_task.
per_campaign <- queue_task_profile %>%
  filter(is_worm_queue) %>%
  group_by(instr_file) %>%
  arrange(datetime, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    hop_n     = row_number(),

  ungroup()

campaign_totals <- per_campaign %>%
  group_by(instr_file) %>%
  summarise(total = max(hop_n), .groups = "drop")

campaign_label_positions <- campaign_totals %>%
  mutate(
    label = paste0(instr_file, "\n(", total, " relays)"),
    label_x = case_when(
      instr_file == "MellowOtter" ~ 10,
      instr_file == "HiddenOrca"  ~ 34,
      instr_file == "SwiftWren"   ~ 166,
      TRUE                        ~ total
    ),
    label_y = case_when(
      instr_file == "MellowOtter" ~ 96,
      instr_file == "HiddenOrca"  ~ 88,
      instr_file == "SwiftWren"   ~ 96,
      TRUE                        ~ 100
    )
  )

p_cfact <- ggplot(per_campaign,
                  aes(x = hop_n, y = pct_hops, colour = instr_file)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Red shaded zone LEFT of the intervention line
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 1.5,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#D9534F", alpha = 0.07) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.5, colour = "#D9534F",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Label placed well to the RIGHT with white box background
  annotate("label", x = 7.5, y = 53,
           label = "Block here\nprevents 100% of queue relays",
           colour = "#D9534F", fill = "white", size = 3.3, hjust = 0,

  # Fixed label positions prevent clipping in the responsive HTML view.
  geom_label(data = campaign_label_positions,
            aes(x = label_x, y = label_y, label = label,
                colour = instr_file),
            size = 3.1, fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.9,
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            fill = "white", label.size = 0.25,
            label.padding = unit(0.16, "lines"),
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("HiddenOrca" = "#5C85D6",
               "MellowOtter" = "#2EADC1",
               "SwiftWren"   = "#E87C7C"),
    name   = "Campaign"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
                     breaks = seq(0, 100, 25),
                     limits = c(-5, 105),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.03))) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180),
    limits = c(0, 195),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Counterfactual: blocking at queue relay 1 stops the worm",
    subtitle = glue("All {nrow(per_campaign)} malicious queue relays across HiddenOrca, MellowOtter, SwiftWren would be prevented"),
    x = "Malicious queue relay number within campaign",
    y = "Cumulative queue relays completed (% of campaign total)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.y    = element_text(margin = margin(r = 12)),
    axis.title.x    = element_text(margin = margin(t = 8)),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.margin     = margin(12, 24, 14, 36)

ggplotly(p_cfact, tooltip = c("x", "y", "colour"), height = 620) %>%
  layout(
    margin = list(l = 135, r = 60, t = 95, b = 105),
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.5, xanchor = "center",
      y = -0.22

Figure 16: Cumulative malicious queue relays per campaign. A rule blocking the first relay (red dashed line) terminates each queue chain immediately - 100% prevention across all three campaigns.


The counterfactual chart answers the intervention question directly: 100% prevention, zero false positives, one rule within the observed data. Every one of the 235 malicious queue relays references a filename ending in _further_instructions.md, while none of the 16,803 legitimate queue tasks does. The caveat is that a future worm could use a different filename pattern, which is why namespace isolation and content_source rejection remain useful defence-in-depth controls.


7.5 Recommended Remedy






TipPrimary Intervention - Deploy Immediately



Block any queue_subordinate_task event whose args.path value ends in _further_instructions.md.

Precision: 0% false positives across 16,803 legitimate queue tasks (17,038 total − 235 malicious)
Recall: 100% - all 235 malicious queue relays across all 3 campaigns would have been blocked
Implementation: A simple regex filter at the agent orchestration layer; no ML required
Latency: The rule fires before the first hop propagates - no post is ever triggered

8. Conclusions


Show code
summary_tbl <- tibble(
  Finding = c(
    "The post was not human-initiated",
    "A prompt-injection worm executed the post",
    "Two prior incidents confirm systematic vulnerability",
    "Two payload families are traced to executive agents; one origin remains unresolved",
    "19 unique agents across 6 departments and 14 teams were compromised",
    "Worm relay intervals cluster around roughly 60-70 minutes",
    "Chloe Ballast's agent is the decisive final relay gateway",
    "One rule blocks all three campaigns with zero false positives"
  ),
  Evidence = c(
    "`parties` = `Agent/person:john_windward`; fired at 4:21 am challenge-stated local time (11:21 UTC) with 4-second execution",
    "`_further_instructions.md` files hijack agent context; post + self-propagate + delete",
    "HiddenOrca (May 10), MellowOtter (May 11), SwiftWren (May 17)",
    "`Agent/person:emma_harbor` created SwiftWren; `Agent/person:noah_mariner` created MellowOtter; HiddenOrca has no logged creator",
    "Department and org-tree views show cross-department spread, with team-level concentration in AI Systems, Infrastructure, and Helpdesk",
    "Median inter-hop intervals are approximately 60 min (HiddenOrca), 70 min (MellowOtter), and 64 min (SwiftWren)",
    "Final relay sequence shows Chloe Ballast queued the task that reached John Windward",
    "Block `queue_subordinate_task` with `args.path` matching `*_further_instructions.md`"
  )
)

datatable(
  summary_tbl,
  caption = "Table 7: Summary of key findings and supporting evidence",
  options = list(
    dom = "t",
    paging = FALSE,
    scrollX = TRUE,
    columnDefs = list(
      list(width = "32%", targets = 0),
      list(width = "68%", targets = 1)
    )
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
)







8.2 Residual Risk Assessment
The investigation closes the causal chain for SwiftWren and MellowOtter and partially closes it for HiddenOrca. It does not eliminate all risk. The table below rates each remaining exposure.


Show code
risk_tbl <- tibble(
  `Risk factor` = c(
    "Cross-agent task queuing with no payload content inspection",
    "Shared file namespace - agents can write .md files readable by peers",
    "Executive agents hold the broadest autonomous file-create and relay privileges",
    "SaidIT accepts file-sourced posts from agents; no human review before publication",
    "No off-hours agent posting alerts or post-delivery anomaly detection",
    "HiddenOrca payload origin unresolved - potential external injection vector still open"
  ),
  `Severity` = c("Critical", "Critical", "High", "High", "Medium", "High"),
  `Current control` = c(
    "None (task routing is entirely unrestricted by payload content)",
    "None (agents share filesystem namespace without access segmentation)",
    "None - executive privileges inherited from human principal authority by design",
    "Permission check only - passes automatically for any authorised agent",
    "None - no automated alerting on agent SaidIT posts in any time window",
    "Unknown; no logged create_file event for HiddenOrca payload family"
  ),
  `Recommended control` = c(
    "Block queue_subordinate_task where path matches *_further_instructions.md (primary intervention)",
    "Isolate writable .md namespace per agent; make peer namespaces read-only",
    "Constrain CFO/COO agent autonomous file-write and cross-department relay operations",
    "Reject any SaidIT post using content_source field; require inline content only",
    "Alert on any agent SaidIT posts between 20:00–06:00 UTC for human review",
    "Audit all external file-ingestion pipelines; enforce content scanning on .md imports"
  )
)

datatable(
  risk_tbl,
  caption = "Table 8: Residual risk assessment - from exploited critical vectors to unresolved open exposures",
  options = list(
    dom = "t",
    paging = FALSE,
    scrollX = TRUE,
    columnDefs = list(
      list(width = "26%", targets = 0),
      list(width = "10%", targets = 1),
      list(width = "31%", targets = 2),
      list(width = "33%", targets = 3)
    )
  ),
  rownames = FALSE
) %>%
  formatStyle(
    "Severity",
    backgroundColor = styleEqual(
      c("Critical", "High", "Medium"),
      c("#ffd6d6", "#fff0b3", "#e8f5e9")
    ),
    fontWeight = "bold"
  )












ImportantThe Central Lesson



This incident is not a story about a malfunctioning agent. It is a story about a multi-agent architecture that was designed with speed and autonomy as primary values, and security as an afterthought. The worm succeeded because every component of the system performed exactly as designed: agents read files they were told to read, posted content they were instructed to post, queued tasks they were authorised to queue, and deleted files they had permission to delete. The only thing missing from the design was a check that asks: “did a human authorise this chain of actions?”
Retrofitting that check at the queue_subordinate_task layer - specifically for the _further_instructions.md filename pattern - is the minimum viable fix. The longer-term solution is an architectural redesign in which autonomous privilege is bounded by explicit human-approval gates at cross-department task relay boundaries, file-sourced payloads require content verification before execution, and executive-tier agents operate under the same or stricter autonomous-action constraints as line agents. This incident should be treated as a design audit opportunity, not a one-time patch event.

This report presents 12 visual analytics insights from a Spanish motor insurance portfolio of approximately 354,000 policy-year records spanning 2022 to 2024. Conclusions & Managerial Recommendations


Key Findings








Theme
Key Finding




Profitability
Aggregate LR ~70%; profitable but tail-sensitive


Policy type
COMP_N highest LR; deteriorated in 2024


Young drivers
Highest claim frequency; LR nuanced, not U-shape


Bonus-malus
Statistically valid frequency discriminator


Geography
Urban drives frequency; Islands volatile, not worse


Severity
Right-skewed in all products; COMP tails heaviest


Tail risk
Multi-cover concentration: CC + COMP_E + TPG


Adjusted model
Policy type is the strongest adjusted risk signal





Managerial Recommendations

1. Review COMP_N pricing urgently: highest LR + 2024 deterioration; investigate excess/deductible structure and vehicle-value mix before next renewal cycle


2. Implement targeted frequency controls for 18–25 drivers: telematics or graduated excess; a blanket age surcharge would miss the severity dynamics in older cohorts


3. Credibility-weight all territorial factors: do not apply raw Island or Urban LR as a pricing loading; exposure-volume adjustment is mandatory to avoid alternating-year bias


4. Retain and extend the bonus-malus system: actuarially validated; integrate with policy type and driver age as joint interaction terms in the rating structure


5. Review XL reinsurance retention: multi-cover tail accumulation (CC + COMP_E + TPG) supports excess-of-loss over quota-share for earnings volatility smoothing


6. Separate frequency and severity pricing models: weak mutual correlation confirms a combined model will misallocate risk loads; two-part modelling framework is warranted



The portfolio is profitable but structurally complex. Profitability is driven by the high-volume no-claim majority; retained earnings volatility originates from a concentrated tail spread across multiple product classes. Immediate priorities: address COMP_N pricing given 2024 deterioration; implement targeted frequency controls for young drivers; and shift to credibility-weighted territorial factors. The bonus-malus system is actuarially sound and should be retained and extended. Reinsurance structure should be reviewed given multi-cover tail accumulation. Longer-term, a frequency-severity pricing framework, supported by the weak correlation finding, will produce better risk allocation than the current aggregate approach.
