                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Distribution of total water point by LGAs")

tmap_arrange(p2, p1, nrow = 1)















Note



Placing the two maps side by side allows for easy comparison between total water points and functional water points per LGA.








TipYour turn



Plot a choropleth map showing the distribution of non-functional water point by LGA.




Show code block
p3 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "wp_nonfunctional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Distribution of non-functional water point by LGAs")

tmap_arrange(p1, p3, nrow = 1)















Note



Comparing the functional and non-functional maps side by side shows that LGAs with a high count of functional water points do not necessarily have a low count of non-functional ones - some LGAs simply have a larger total number of water points overall, so both counts are high. This is exactly why a rate map (covered next) is more informative than mapping raw counts.

title: Analytical Mapping
text:
4. Choropleth Map for Rates

4.1 Deriving Proportion of Functional and Non-Functional Water Points
Mapping absolute counts can be misleading because the number of water points varies spatially across LGAs. A rate map, which shows the proportion of functional or non-functional water points, is more informative.
The code chunk below uses mutate() of the dplyr package to derive two new variables, pct_functional and pct_nonfunctional.


Show code block
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional / total_wp) %>%
  mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional / total_wp)




4.2 Plotting the Rate Map






TipYour turn



Plot a choropleth map showing the distribution of percentage functional water point by LGA.


The code chunk below is used to plot a choropleth map showing the rate of functional water points.


Show code block
tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons("pct_functional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Rate map of functional water point by LGAs")















Note



Unlike the absolute count maps in Section 3, this rate map controls for the total number of water points in each LGA. LGAs that appeared “high” in the functional count map earlier are not necessarily the ones with the best functional rate - some simply have more water points overall. The rate map gives a fairer, more meaningful basis for comparing LGAs.

title: Analytical Mapping
text:
5. Extreme Value Maps
Extreme value maps are variations of common choropleth maps where the classification is designed to highlight extreme values at the lower and upper ends of the scale, with the goal of identifying outliers.

5.1 Percentile Map
The percentile map uses a special quantile classification scheme with six categories: 0–1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, and 99–100%.

5.1.1 Data Preparation
Step 1: Exclude records with NA values


Show code block
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()


Step 2: Create the customised classification and inspect quantile values


Show code block
percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[, 1], percent)


       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 








Note



When variables are extracted from an sf data frame, the geometry column is included by default. The st_set_geometry(NULL) function removes the geometry so that base R functions like quantile() can operate on the numeric values directly.




5.1.2 Why Write Functions?
The section on percentile maps requires the same sequence of operations to be performed each time we want to create this type of map for a different variable. Writing functions helps to:

give the code a meaningful name,
maintain all the logic in a single place, and
eliminate repetitive copy-and-paste errors.

Source: Chapter 19: Functions of R for Data Science.


5.1.3 Creating the get.var Function
The get.var() function is used to extract a field as a vector from an sf data frame.


Show code block
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}








Note




vname is the variable name as a character string.
df is the sf data frame.
The function returns the values as a plain vector without names.





5.1.4 A Percentile Mapping Function
The code chunk below defines the percentmap() function, which builds a percentile choropleth map for any variable in the data frame.


Show code block
percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(vnam,
                title = legtitle,
                breaks = bperc,
                palette = "Blues",
                labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                           "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("right", "bottom"))
}




5.1.5 Testing the Percentile Mapping Function


Show code block
percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)












5.2 Box Map
A box map is an augmented quartile map with an additional lower and upper category. When there are lower outliers, the map breaks the first class into two: a lower outlier class and a below Q1 class. When there are upper outliers, the map breaks the last class into two: an above Q3 class and an upper outlier class.
The code chunk below is used to create a boxplot to explore the distribution of the wp_nonfunctional variable.


Show code block
ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()










5.2.1 Creating the boxbreaks Function
The boxbreaks() function is used to compute the break points for the box map.


Show code block
boxbreaks <- function(v, mult = 1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  bb <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = 7)
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) {
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}








Note




v is a vector of observations.
mult is the multiplier for the IQR, which defaults to 1.5.
The function returns a vector of 7 breakpoints that account for the presence or absence of lower and upper outliers.





5.2.2 Creating the get.var Function
The same get.var() function defined earlier is used here again to extract variable values from the sf data frame.


Show code block
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}




5.2.3 Testing the boxbreaks Function


Show code block
var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)
boxbreaks(var)


[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0




5.2.4 Boxmap Function
The boxmap() function creates the final box map visualisation using the break points computed by boxbreaks().


Show code block
boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle = NA,
                   mtitle = "Box Map",
                   mult = 1.5) {
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,
            title = legtitle,
            breaks = bb,
            palette = "Blues",
            labels = c("lower outlier",
                       "< 25%",
                       "25% - 50%",
                       "50% - 75%",
                       "> 75%",
                       "upper outlier")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("left", "top"))
}

tmap_mode("plot")
boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)















Note




vnam is the variable name (character string).
df is the simple features polygon layer.
legtitle is the legend title.
mtitle is the map title.
mult is the multiplier for the IQR (default 1.5).

title: Analytical Mapping
text:
6. Reference

Kam, T.S. (2023). Chapter 23: Analytical Mapping. R for Visual Analytics.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
1. Learning Outcome
By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will be able to:

import geospatial and attribute data into R using appropriate R methods,
convert imported data into appropriate simple feature data frames,
perform a relational join to merge both data sets,
create choropleth maps using the tmap package, and
apply different data classification methods and colour schemes to enhance choropleth maps.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
2. Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading R Packages
The R packages required for this exercise are: sf, tmap, and tidyverse. The code chunk below uses pacman::p_load() to check, install, and load all the necessary packages.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
3. Importing Data into R

3.1 The Data
Two data sets will be used in this exercise:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) in ESRI shapefile format, which provides the geospatial information of Singapore’s planning subzones.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2000–2020 in csv format (respopagesextod2011to2020.csv), which provides the attribute data on population.



3.2 Importing Geospatial Data into R
The code chunk below uses st_read() of the sf package to import the shapefile into R as a simple feature data frame called mpsz.


Show code block
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W9/MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL",
                layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")

Notice that only the first ten records will be displayed. Do you know why?
This is because mpsz is also a tibble data frame, and by default, R only prints the first 10 rows of a tibble to keep the console output readable. The same truncation behaviour will be seen whenever a large tibble or sf object is printed without head() or explicit row limits.




3.3 Importing Attribute Data into R
Next, I will import respopagesextod2011to2020.csv into RStudio as a tibble data frame called popdata.


Show code block
popdata <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W9/respopagesextod2011to2020.csv")




3.4 Data Preparation
Before a choropleth map can be prepared, a data table with values at the planning subzone level is required. The data table should include the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, and DEPENDENCY.

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 until age group 20 to 24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25 to 29 until age group 60 to 64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age groups, and
DEPENDENCY: ratio of (YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY ACTIVE.


3.4.1 Data Wrangling
The following data wrangling and transformation functions will be used:

pivot_wider() of the tidyr package, and
mutate(), filter(), group_by(), and select() of the dplyr package.



Show code block
popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG,
              values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6]) + rowSums(.[12])) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11]) + rowSums(.[13:15])) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)




3.4.2 Joining Attribute and Geospatial Data
Before performing the georelational join, I need to convert the values of the PA and SZ fields to uppercase so they match the values in the geospatial data.


Show code block
popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


Next, left_join() is used to merge the geographical data and the attribute table using the planning subzone name as the common identifier.


Show code block
mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))




Show code block
write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W9/mpszpop2020.rds")








Note



left_join() of the dplyr package is used with mpsz as the left data table to ensure that all the planning subzones in Singapore are retained.

title: Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4. Choropleth Mapping Using tmap
Two approaches can be used to prepare a choropleth map using tmap:

Plotting a thematic map quickly by using qtm(), and
Plotting a highly customisable thematic map by using tmap elements.


4.1 Plotting a Choropleth Map Quickly Using qtm()
The easiest and quickest way to draw a choropleth map using tmap is qtm(). It is concise and provides a good default visualisation in many cases.


Show code block
tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020, fill = "DEPENDENCY")















Note




tmap_mode() with the “plot” option is used to produce a static map. For an interactive mode, the “view” option should be used.
The fill argument is used to map the attribute DEPENDENCY.





4.2 Creating a Choropleth Map Using tmap Elements
Despite its usefulness for drawing a choropleth map quickly and easily, the drawback of qtm() is that it makes aesthetic control of individual layers harder. To draw a high-quality cartographic choropleth map, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

4.2.1 Drawing a Base Map
The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elements such as tm_fill() and tm_polygons().


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()











4.2.2 Drawing a Choropleth Map Using tm_polygons()
To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, I just need to assign the target variable such as DEPENDENCY to tm_polygons().


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")















Note




The default interval binning used to draw the choropleth map is called “pretty”.
The default colour scheme used is YlOrRd of ColorBrewer.
By default, missing values will be shaded in grey.





4.2.3 Drawing a Choropleth Map Using tm_fill() and tm_borders()
tm_polygons() is a wrapper of tm_fill() and tm_borders(). tm_fill() shades the polygons using the default colour scheme, while tm_borders() adds the borders of the shapefile onto the choropleth map.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01, fill_alpha = 0.1)















Note



The alpha argument is used to define transparency as a number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the colour is used (normally 1).





4.3 Data Classification Methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps employ some method of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes.
tmap provides ten data classification methods, namely: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.






WarningWarning: Maps Lie!



The choice of classification method and number of classes can dramatically change the message a choropleth map conveys, even though the underlying data has not changed at all. The same variable can be made to look almost uniform or highly polarised purely by adjusting these two settings. As a map maker, I need to be deliberate and transparent about the classification method and number of classes I choose, since these decisions can unintentionally (or intentionally) mislead readers.



4.3.1 Plotting Choropleth Maps with Built-in Classification Methods
The code chunk below shows a quantile data classification that uses 5 classes.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









The code chunk below shows an equal data classification that uses 5 classes.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









The code chunk below shows a Jenks natural breaks classification that uses 5 classes.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











4.3.2 Plotting Choropleth Maps with Custom Break Points
Besides the built-in data classification methods, breakpoints can also be set explicitly by means of the breaks argument. It is good practice to get some descriptive statistics on the variable before setting the breakpoints.


Show code block
summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 


With reference to the summary statistics above, I will set break points at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90. In addition, I need to include a minimum and maximum, which I will set at 0 and 1.00. The breaks vector is thus c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00).


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











4.3.3 DIY: Comparing Different Classification Methods






TipDIY



Using what I had learned, prepare choropleth maps by using different classification methods supported by tmap and compare their differences.


To answer this, I will plot maps using five different classification methods—jenks, quantile, equal, sd, and fisher—all keeping n = 5, side by side for comparison.


Show code block
map_jenks <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Jenks")

map_quantile <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Quantile")

map_equal <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Equal")

map_sd <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "sd", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Standard Deviation")

map_fisher <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "fisher", n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Fisher")

tmap_arrange(map_jenks, map_quantile, map_equal, map_sd, map_fisher, ncol = 3)















NoteMy observations




Jenks and fisher produce very similar maps because both methods minimise within-class variance and tend to find natural breaks/clusters in the data — subzones with extreme dependency ratios stand out clearly as their own class.
Quantile forces an equal number of subzones (roughly 1/5 of the total) into each class, so the map looks the most “balanced” even though the underlying values within each class can vary widely. This can hide the fact that most subzones actually have similar dependency ratios.
Equal divides the value range into 5 equally-sized intervals regardless of how the data points are distributed. Because DEPENDENCY is right-skewed, most subzones fall into just one or two of the lower classes, making the map look almost monochrome.
Standard deviation centres the classes on the mean, so it is most useful for showing which subzones are above or below average, but it is harder to interpret for readers unfamiliar with the method.
Overall, the same data can tell quite different visual stories depending on the classification method chosen — this is exactly the risk highlighted in the “Maps Lie!” warning above.





4.3.4 DIY: Comparing Different Numbers of Classes






TipDIY



Prepare choropleth maps by using a similar classification method but with different numbers of classes (i.e. 2, 6, 10, 20). Compare the output maps. What observation can you draw?


I will hold the classification method constant at “pretty” and vary the number of classes (n) to 2, 6, 10, and 20.


Show code block
map_n2 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 2")

map_n6 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 6")

map_n10 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 10)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 10")

map_n20 <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 20)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("n = 20")

tmap_arrange(map_n2, map_n6, map_n10, map_n20, ncol = 2)















NoteMy observations




With n = 2, the map only distinguishes “high” versus “low” dependency subzones. This is the most generalised view and hides almost all spatial nuance — many genuinely different subzones get lumped into the same broad class.
As n increases to 6 and 10, finer spatial patterns start to emerge — clusters of planning subzones with similarly high or low dependency ratios become visible, and the map begins to reveal local variation that the 2-class version completely missed.
At n = 20, the map becomes very granular. While this preserves more detail, it also becomes harder to read at a glance: many classes share visually similar colours, the legend becomes long and unwieldy, and individual classes may contain very few subzones (or none at all), reducing the map’s communicative value.
The overall takeaway is that there is a trade-off between detail and readability: too few classes oversimplify and can mask meaningful variation, while too many classes overwhelm the reader and dilute the visual signal. A moderate number of classes (typically 5–7) tends to strike the best balance for most choropleth maps.






4.4 Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps either defined by the user or a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

4.4.1 Using ColorBrewer Palette
To change the colour, I assign the preferred colour scheme to the values argument of tm_scale_intervals().


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









To reverse the colour shading, I add a “-” prefix to the colour scheme name.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)












4.5 Map Layouts
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohesive map. Map elements include objects to be mapped, the title, the scale bar, the compass, margins, and aspect ratios.

4.5.1 Map Legend
In tmap, several legend options are provided to change the placement, format, and appearance of the legend.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone\n(Jenks classification)")











4.5.2 Map Style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed. They can be called by using tmap_style().


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")











4.5.3 Cartographic Furniture
tmap also provides arguments to draw other map furniture such as compass, scale bar, and grid lines.
In the code chunk below, tm_compass(), tm_grid(), and tm_credits() are used to add a compass rose, grid lines, and attribution text onto the choropleth map.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\nand Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









To reset the default style, the code chunk below is used.


Show code block
tmap_style("white")





4.6 Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also referred to as facet maps, are composed of many maps arranged side by side, and sometimes stacked vertically. Small multiple maps enable the visualisation of how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time.
In tmap, small multiple maps can be plotted in three ways:

by assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments,
by defining a group-by variable in tm_facets(), and
by creating multiple standalone maps with tmap_arrange().


4.6.1 By Assigning Multiple Values to at Least One Aesthetic Argument
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning multiple values to tm_fill().


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal",
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")









In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning multiple values along with different classification methods.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(c("DEPENDENCY", "AGED"),
              style = c("equal", "quantile"),
              palette = list("Blues", "Greens")) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))











4.6.2 By Defining a Group-by Variable in tm_facets()
In this example, multiple small maps are created using tm_facets().


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          thres.poly = 0) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            free.coords = TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = FALSE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"),
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)











4.6.3 By Creating Multiple Standalone Maps with tmap_arrange()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created by using tmap_arrange().


Show code block
youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("YOUNG",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("AGED",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)












4.7 Mapping Spatial Objects Meeting Selection Criteria
Instead of creating small multiple choropleth maps, the selection function can be used to map spatial objects that meet a specified selection criterion.


Show code block
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020[mpsz_pop2020$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION", ]) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          legend.hist = TRUE,
          legend.is.portrait = TRUE,
          legend.hist.z = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE,
            legend.height = 0.45,
            legend.width = 5.0,
            legend.position = c("right", "bottom"),
            frame = FALSE) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
1. Learning Outcome
In this hands-on exercise, I will learn how to visualise and analyse text data using R. By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will be able to:

understand the tidytext framework for processing, analysing and visualising text data,
write a function for importing multiple files into R,
combine multiple files into a single data frame,
clean and wrangle text data by using a tidyverse approach,
visualise words with Word Cloud,
compute term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) using tidytext methods, and
visualise texts and terms relationships.

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
2. Getting Started

Installing and loading the packagesReading the data


For this exercise, the following R packages for handling, processing, wrangling, analysing and visualising text data will be used:

tidytext and tidyverse (mainly readr, purrr, stringr, ggplot2),
widyr,
wordcloud and ggwordcloud,
textplot (which requires igraph, tidygraph and ggraph),
DT, and
lubridate and hms.

The code chunk below installs and loads all required packages into the R environment.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(tidytext, widyr, wordcloud, DT, ggwordcloud, textplot, lubridate, hms,
               tidyverse, tidygraph, ggraph, igraph)




For this exercise, I will use the 20 Newsgroups dataset. It consists of approximately 20,000 newsgroup messages partitioned across 20 different newsgroups.
The raw data is stored in the data/20news/ sub-folder. I will import and process it in Section 4 below, then read the saved RDS file going forward.

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: 3. Importing Multiple Text Files from Multiple Folders
text:
3. Importing Multiple Text Files from Multiple Folders

3.1 Creating a Folder List
I will first define the path to the 20 newsgroups dataset folder.


Show code block
news20 <- "Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W7/20news"




3.2 Defining a Function to Read All Files from a Folder into a Data Frame
Next, I will define a read_folder() function that reads all text files from a given folder into a data frame.


Show code block
read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder,
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file,
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file),
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
section: 4. Reading in All the Messages from the 20news Folder
text:
4. Reading in All the Messages from the 20news Folder
Using read_folder(), I will now read all messages from every newsgroup sub-folder, combine them into a single data frame, and save the result as an RDS file for future use.


Show code block
raw_text <- tibble(folder =
                     dir(news20,
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder,
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder),
            id, text)
write_rds(raw_text, "Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W7/news20.rds")








NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




read_lines() of the readr package is used to read up to n_max lines from a file.
map() of the purrr package transforms input by applying a function to each element of a list and returns an object of the same length as the input.
unnest() of the dplyr package flattens a list-column of data frames back out into regular columns.
mutate() of dplyr adds new variables while preserving existing ones.
transmute() of dplyr adds new variables while dropping existing ones.
write_rds() saves the extracted and combined data frame as an RDS file for future use.

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
5. Initial EDA
I will load the saved RDS file and visualise the frequency of messages by newsgroup.


Show code block
raw_text <- read_rds("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W7/news20.rds")
raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarize(messages = n_distinct(id)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(messages, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(y = NULL)

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
6. Introducing tidytext
By using tidy data principles for text data, I can take advantage of the existing infrastructure in packages like dplyr, broom, tidyr, and ggplot2.


6.1 Removing Header and Automated Email Signatures
Each message contains structure I don’t want in my analysis — headers (fields like “from:” or “in_reply_to:”) and automated email signatures (after a line like “––”). The code chunk below removes these.


Show code block
cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()








NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




cumsum() of base R returns a vector whose elements are the cumulative sums of the elements of the argument.
str_detect() from stringr detects the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.





6.2 Removing Lines with Nested Text Representing Quotes from Other Users
Next, I will use regular expressions to remove lines containing quoted text from other users.


Show code block
cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text,
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text,
                     "^In article <")
  )








NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




str_detect() from stringr detects the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.
filter() of the dplyr package subsets a data frame, retaining all rows that satisfy the specified conditions.





6.3 Text Data Processing
In the code chunk below, unnest_tokens() of the tidytext package is used to split the dataset into tokens, while stop_words is used to remove stop words.


Show code block
usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)


Now that I’ve removed the headers, signatures, and formatting, I can start exploring common words. I will first find the most common words in the entire dataset.


Show code block
usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)


# A tibble: 5,542 × 2
   word           n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 people        57
 2 time          50
 3 jesus         47
 4 god           44
 5 message       40
 6 br            27
 7 bible         23
 8 drive         23
 9 homosexual    23
10 read          22
# ℹ 5,532 more rows


I can also count words within each newsgroup separately.


Show code block
words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()




6.4 Visualising Words in Newsgroups — Static Word Cloud
In the code chunk below, wordcloud() of the wordcloud package is used to plot a static word cloud.


Show code block
wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)











6.5 Visualising Words in Newsgroups — ggwordcloud
I will now use the ggwordcloud package to create faceted word clouds, one per newsgroup.


Show code block
set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
ggplot(aes(label = word,
           size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)

title: Visualising and Analysing Text Data with R: tidytext methods
text:
7. Basic Concept of TF-IDF
TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) is a numerical statistic that reflects how important a word is to a document within a collection or corpus.


7.1 Computing TF-IDF within Newsgroups
The code chunk below uses bind_tf_idf() of the tidytext package to compute and bind the term frequency, inverse document frequency, and TF-IDF values to the dataset.


Show code block
tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))




7.2 Visualising TF-IDF as an Interactive Table
I will use datatable() of the DT package to create an interactive HTML table.


Show code block
DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = 'top') %>%
  formatRound(columns = c('tf', 'idf',
                          'tf_idf'),
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0,
              target = 'row',
              lineHeight='25%')












NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




The filter argument controls the filter UI in the rendered table.
formatRound() customises the value format; the digits argument defines the number of decimal places.
formatStyle() customises the output table. Here, target and lineHeight reduce the row height by 25%.





7.3 Visualising TF-IDF within Newsgroups
I will use facet bar charts to visualise the top TF-IDF terms for science-related newsgroups.


Show code block
tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf,
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word,
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf,
             word,
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup,
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf",
       y = NULL)











7.4 Counting and Correlating Pairs of Words with widyr
To see how correlated newsgroups are based on the words they share, I will use pairwise_cor() of the widyr package. The widyr package first casts a tidy dataset into a wide matrix, performs the operation (e.g., correlation), then re-tidies the result.



Show code block
newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup,
               word,
               n,
               sort = TRUE)




7.5 Visualising Correlation as a Network
I will now visualise the relationships between newsgroups in a network graph using graph_from_data_frame() of igraph and ggraph().


Show code block
set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation,
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6,
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()











7.6 Bigrams
I will now analyse word pairs (bigrams) using unnest_tokens() of tidytext with token = "ngrams" and n = 2.


Show code block
bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram,
                text,
                token = "ngrams",
                n = 2)
bigrams


# A tibble: 28,824 × 3
   newsgroup   id    bigram    
   <chr>       <chr> <chr>     
 1 alt.atheism 54256 <NA>      
 2 alt.atheism 54256 <NA>      
 3 alt.atheism 54256 as i      
 4 alt.atheism 54256 i don't   
 5 alt.atheism 54256 don't know
 6 alt.atheism 54256 know this 
 7 alt.atheism 54256 this book 
 8 alt.atheism 54256 book i    
 9 alt.atheism 54256 i will    
10 alt.atheism 54256 will use  
# ℹ 28,814 more rows




7.7 Counting Bigrams
I will count and sort the bigrams.


Show code block
bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)
bigrams_count


# A tibble: 19,885 × 2
   bigram       n
   <chr>    <int>
 1 of the     169
 2 in the     113
 3 to the      74
 4 to be       59
 5 for the     52
 6 i have      48
 7 that the    47
 8 if you      40
 9 on the      39
10 it is       38
# ℹ 19,875 more rows




7.8 Cleaning Bigrams
I will separate each bigram into two individual words and filter out stop words from both.


Show code block
bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"),
           sep = " ")

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)
bigrams_filtered


# A tibble: 4,604 × 4
   newsgroup   id    word1        word2        
   <chr>       <chr> <chr>        <chr>        
 1 alt.atheism 54256 defines      god          
 2 alt.atheism 54256 term         preclues     
 3 alt.atheism 54256 science      ideas        
 4 alt.atheism 54256 ideas        drawn        
 5 alt.atheism 54256 supernatural precludes    
 6 alt.atheism 54256 scientific   assertions   
 7 alt.atheism 54256 religious    dogma        
 8 alt.atheism 54256 religion     involves     
 9 alt.atheism 54256 involves     circumventing
10 alt.atheism 54256 gain         absolute     
# ℹ 4,594 more rows




7.9 Counting Bigrams Again
After cleaning, I will recount the bigrams to get meaningful word pair frequencies.


Show code block
bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)




7.10 Creating a Network Graph from Bigram Data Frame
I will create a directed network graph from the bigram counts using graph_from_data_frame() of the igraph package.


Show code block
bigram_graph <- bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()
bigram_graph


IGRAPH 2befac6 DN-- 40 24 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), n (e/n)
+ edges from 2befac6 (vertex names):
 [1] 1          ->2           1          ->3           static     ->void       
 [4] time       ->pad         1          ->4           infield    ->fly        
 [7] mat        ->28          vv         ->vv          1          ->5          
[10] cock       ->crow        noticeshell->widget      27         ->1993       
[13] 3          ->4           child      ->molestation cock       ->crew       
[16] gun        ->violence    heat       ->sink        homosexual ->male       
[19] homosexual ->women       include    ->xol         mary       ->magdalene  
[22] read       ->write       rev        ->20          tt         ->ee         




7.11 Visualising a Network of Bigrams with ggraph
I will plot a basic network visualisation of the bigrams.


Show code block
set.seed(1234)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point() +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 vjust = 1,
                 hjust = 1)











7.12 Revised Version
Finally, I will create a more polished version of the bigram network graph by adding directional arrows and visual styling.


Show code block
set.seed(1234)

a <- grid::arrow(type = "closed",
                 length = unit(.15,
                               "inches"))

ggraph(bigram_graph,
       layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07,
                                  'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue",
                  size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 vjust = 1,
                 hjust = 1) +
  theme_void()

title: Treemap Visualisation with R
text: In this hands-on exercise, I will gain hands-on experience designing treemaps using appropriate R packages. The exercise consists of three main sections. First, I will manipulate transaction data into a treemap structure using selected functions from the dplyr package. Then, I will plot static treemaps using the treemap package. In the third section, I will design interactive treemaps using the d3treeR package.

title: Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
2. Installing and Launching R Packages
I will first check and load the treemap, treemapify, and tidyverse packages.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, tidyverse)

title: Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
3. Data Wrangling
In this exercise, I will use the REALIS2018.csv data, which provides information on private property transaction records in 2018. The dataset is extracted from the REALIS portal of the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).

3.1 Importing the Data Set
I will use read_csv() of readr to import realis2018.csv into R and parse it into a tibble data frame.


Show code block
realis2018 <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W5/realis2018.csv")




3.2 Data Wrangling and Manipulation
The realis2018 data frame is in transaction record form — highly disaggregated and not appropriate for plotting a treemap. I will perform the following steps:

Group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type, and Type of Sale.
Compute Total Unit Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price, and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics.

I will use two key dplyr verbs: group_by() and summarise().
group_by() breaks down a data frame into specified groups of rows, after which verbs are automatically applied “by group”. summarise() computes the summary for each group.


3.3 Grouped Summaries without the Pipe
The code chunk below shows a two-line approach to perform the steps.


Show code block
realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`,
                               `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped,
                          `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))








Note



Aggregation functions such as sum() and median() follow the usual rule of missing values — if there’s any missing value in the input, the output will be missing. The argument na.rm = TRUE removes missing values prior to computation.




3.4 Grouped Summaries with the Pipe
A more efficient way to tackle the same process is using the pipe %>%:


Show code block
realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>%
  group_by(`Project Name`, `Planning Region`,
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`,
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

title: Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
4. Designing Treemap with treemap Package
The treemap package is specially designed to offer great flexibility in drawing treemaps. The core function treemap() offers at least 43 arguments. In this section, I will explore the major arguments for designing elegant and truthful treemaps.

4.1 Designing a Static Treemap
In this section, I will use treemap() to plot a treemap showing the distribution of median unit prices and total unit sold of resale condominiums by geographic hierarchy in 2018.
First, I will filter records belonging to resale condominium property type:


Show code block
realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", `Type of Sale` == "Resale")




4.2 Using the Basic Arguments
The code chunk below designs a treemap using the three core arguments: index, vSize, and vColor.


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )









Things to note:

index: the index vector must consist of at least two column names, otherwise no hierarchy treemap will be plotted. The first name is the highest aggregation level.
vSize: the column must not contain negative values, as its values map to the sizes of the rectangles.







Warning



The treemap above was wrongly coloured. For a correctly designed treemap, the colours of the rectangles should be in different intensities showing median unit prices. Without defining type, treemap() assumes type = index, meaning it colours by the hierarchy of planning areas.




4.3 Working with vColor and type Arguments
I will now define the type argument as "value" for correct colouring:


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )









The rectangles are now coloured with different intensities of green, reflecting their respective median unit prices. The legend shows values binned into ten equal intervals of 5,000.


4.4 Colours in treemap Package
Two arguments determine the mapping to colour palettes: mapping and palette. The "value" treemap treats the palette as diverging (e.g. "RdYlBu"), mapping 0 to the middle colour, while "manual" maps min(values) to the left-end colour and max(values) to the right-end colour.


4.5 The “value” Type Treemap


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        palette = "RdYlBu",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )









Note that although the RdYlBu palette is used, there are no red rectangles — because all median unit prices are positive.


4.6 The “manual” Type Treemap
The "manual" type maps the value range linearly to the colour palette:


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "RdYlBu",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )









The colour scheme is confusing here because a diverging palette like RdYlBu is not wise when all values are positive. I will use a single colour palette instead:


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











4.7 Treemap Layout
treemap() supports two popular treemap layouts: "squarified" and "pivotSize". The default is "pivotSize". The squarified algorithm (Bruls et al., 2000) produces good aspect ratios but ignores sorting order, while the pivot-by-size algorithm (Bederson et al., 2002) takes sorting order into account.


4.8 Working with algorithm Argument
The code chunk below plots a squarified treemap:


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues",
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











4.9 Using sortID
When "pivotSize" algorithm is used, the sortID argument determines the order in which rectangles are placed from top-left to bottom-right.


Show code block
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues",
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )

title: Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
5. Designing Treemap using treemapify Package
treemapify is specially developed to draw treemaps in ggplot2. Before getting started, I recommend reading the Introduction to treemapify and its user guide.

5.1 Designing a Basic Treemap


Show code block
ggplot(data = realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`),
       layout = "scol",
       start = "bottomleft") +
  geom_treemap() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "light blue", high = "blue")











5.2 Defining Hierarchy
Group by Planning Region:


Show code block
ggplot(data = realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`),
       start = "topleft") +
  geom_treemap()









Group by Planning Area:


Show code block
ggplot(data = realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) +
  geom_treemap()









Adding boundary lines:


Show code block
ggplot(data = realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "gray40",
                                size = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "gray20")

title: Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
6. Designing Interactive Treemap using d3treeR

6.1 Installing d3treeR Package
d3treeR is not available on CRAN. I will install it from GitHub as follows:

# Step 1: Install devtools if not already installed
install.packages("devtools")

# Step 2: Load devtools and install d3treeR from GitHub

The code below performs two steps:

tm <- treemap(realis2018_summarised,

d3tree(tm, rootname = "Singapore")

title: Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
Heatmaps visualise data through variations in colouring. When applied to a tabular format, heatmaps are useful for cross-examining multivariate data by placing variables in the columns and observations (or records) in rows, and colouring the cells within the table. Heatmaps are good for showing variance across multiple variables, revealing patterns, displaying whether variables are similar to each other, and detecting correlations in-between them.
In this hands-on exercise, I will gain hands-on experience using R to plot both static and interactive heatmaps for visualising and analysing multivariate data.

title: Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
2. Installing and Launching R Packages

title: Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
section: 3. Importing and Preparing the Data Set
text:
3. Importing and Preparing the Data Set
In this hands-on exercise, I will use the World Happiness 2018 report data. The data set has been extracted from the original Excel file and saved as WHData-2018.csv.

3.1 Importing the Data Set
I will use read_csv() of readr to import WHData-2018.csv into R and parse it into a tibble data frame.


Show code block
wh <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W5/WHData-2018.csv")




3.2 Preparing the Data
Next, I need to change the rows to use country names instead of row numbers.


Show code block
row.names(wh) <- wh$Country




3.3 Transforming the Data Frame into a Matrix
The data was loaded into a data frame, but it must be a data matrix to make a heatmap. I will use the code chunk below to transform the wh data frame into a data matrix.


Show code block
wh1 <- dplyr::select(wh, c(3, 7:12))
wh_matrix <- data.matrix(wh)

title: Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
4. Static Heatmap
There are several R packages and functions I can use to draw static heatmaps:

heatmap() of R stats — draws a simple heatmap.
heatmap.2() of gplots — an enhanced heatmap compared to the R base function.
pheatmap() of pheatmap — also known as Pretty Heatmap, with more control over appearance.
ComplexHeatmap of R/Bioconductor — very useful for genomic data analysis.
superheat — a graphical tool for exploring complex datasets, including big data and data with multiple data types.

In this section, I will plot static heatmaps using heatmap() of the R Stats package.

4.1 heatmap() of R Stats
I will plot a heatmap using heatmap() of Base Stats. The code chunk below switches off the row and column dendrograms using Rowv=NA and Colv=NA.


Show code block
wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      Rowv=NA, Colv=NA)









To plot a cluster heatmap, I just use the default settings:


Show code block
wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix)









Note that the order of both rows and columns differs from the native wh_matrix because heatmap reorders by clusterisation — calculating distances between each pair of rows and columns and ordering them by similarity. The corresponding dendrogram is displayed alongside the heatmap.
The red cells denote small values. This heatmap is not very informative because the Happiness Score variable has relatively higher values, making the other variables with small values look identical. I need to normalise the matrix using the scale argument.
The code chunk below normalises the matrix column-wise:


Show code block
wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale = "column",
                      cexRow = 0.6,
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))









The margins argument ensures x-axis labels are displayed completely, while cexRow and cexCol control the font size of the y-axis and x-axis labels respectively.

title: Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5. Creating Interactive Heatmap
heatmaply is an R package for building interactive cluster heatmaps that can be shared online as standalone HTML files.
Before getting started, I recommend reviewing the Introduction to Heatmaply and keeping the user manual handy for reference.

5.1 Working with heatmaply


Show code block
heatmaply(mtcars)






The code chunk below shows the basic syntax for creating an interactive heatmap using heatmaply.


Show code block
heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])






Note that:

Unlike heatmap(), the default horizontal dendrogram in heatmaply() is placed on the left-hand side.
The text label of each row is placed on the right-hand side.
When x-axis marker labels are too long, they are rotated by 135 degrees from the north.



5.2 Data Transformation
When analysing multivariate data sets, variables often reflect different types of measurements with different ranges. To ensure all variables have comparable values, I will apply data transformation before clustering. heatmaply() supports three main methods: scale, normalise, and percentise.

5.2.1 Scaling Method
When all variables come from (or are assumed to come from) a normal distribution, scaling — subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation — brings them to the standard normal distribution. The code chunk below scales variable values column-wise.


Show code block
heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")








5.2.2 Normalising Method
When variables come from possibly different (and non-normal) distributions, the normalize function brings data to the 0–1 scale by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the maximum. This preserves each variable’s distribution shape while making them comparable.


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))








5.2.3 Percentising Method
Similar to ranking, percentising uses the empirical CDF of each variable’s values, bringing each observation to its empirical percentile. Each value can then be interpreted as the percentage of observations at or below it.


Show code block
heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))









5.3 Clustering Algorithm
heatmaply supports a variety of hierarchical clustering algorithms. The main arguments are:

distfun: function used to compute distance between rows and columns. Defaults to dist. Supports "pearson", "spearman", and "kendall" for correlation-based clustering.
hclustfun: function used to compute hierarchical clustering. Defaults to hclust.
dist_method: defaults to "euclidean". Can also be "maximum", "manhattan", "canberra", "binary", or "minkowski".
hclust_method: defaults to "complete". Can also be "ward.D", "ward.D2", "single", "average", "mcquitty", "median", or "centroid".



5.4 Manual Approach
In the code chunk below, I plot the heatmap using hierarchical clustering with "euclidean" distance and "ward.D" method.


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D")








5.5 Statistical Approach
To determine the best clustering method and number of clusters, I will use dend_expend() and find_k() of the dendextend package.
First, dend_expend() helps me determine the recommended clustering method:


Show code block
wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]


  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6137851
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6289186
3      unknown         single 0.4774362
4      unknown       complete 0.6434009
5      unknown        average 0.6701688
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.5020102
7      unknown         median 0.5901833
8      unknown       centroid 0.6338734


The output table shows that the "average" method should be used as it gives the highest optimum value.
Next, find_k() helps me determine the optimal number of clusters:


Show code block
wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)









The figure above shows that k=3 would be a good choice. With reference to these results, I prepare the code chunk below:


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)








5.6 Seriation
One challenge with hierarchical clustering is that it doesn’t place rows in a definite order — it merely constrains the space of possible orderings. heatmaply uses the seriation package to find an optimal ordering of rows and columns by minimising the Hamiltonian path length restricted by the dendrogram structure.
Here I apply the Optimal Leaf Ordering (OLO) algorithm:


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "OLO")






The "GW" (Gruvaeus and Wainer) option aims for the same goal using a potentially faster heuristic:


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "GW")






The "mean" option produces the same output as heatmap functions in other packages such as gplots::heatmap.2:


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "mean")






The "none" option produces dendrograms without any rotation:


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none")








5.7 Working with Colour Palettes
The default colour palette in heatmaply is viridis. I can use other palettes to improve the aesthetics and visual friendliness of the heatmap. Below I use the Blues palette from RColorBrewer:


Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues)








5.8 The Finishing Touch
Besides statistical analysis arguments, heatmaply also provides many plotting features for producing cartographic quality heatmaps. In the code chunk below, I use the following arguments:

k_row: to produce 5 groups.
margins: to change the top margin to 60 and row margin to 200.
fontsize_row and fontsize_col: to change font size for row and column labels to 4 and 5 respectively.
main: to write the main title of the plot.
xlab and ylab: to write the x-axis and y-axis labels.



Show code block
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          Colv = NA,
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 5,
          margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main = "World Happiness Score and Variables by Country, 2018 \nData Transformation using Normalise Method",
          xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
          ylab = "World Countries"
          )

title: Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
1. Overview
Ternary plots are a way of displaying the distribution and variability of three-part compositional data. For example, the proportion of aged, economy active and young population, or sand, silt, and clay in soil. The display is a triangle with sides scaled from 0 to 1. Each side represents one of the three components. A point is plotted so that a line drawn perpendicular from the point to each leg of the triangle intersects at the component values of the point.
In this hands-on exercise, I will build ternary plots programmatically using R to visualise and analyse the population structure of Singapore.
My hands-on exercise consists of four steps:

I will install and launch tidyverse and ggtern packages.
I will derive three new measures using the mutate() function of the dplyr package.
I will build a static ternary plot using the ggtern() function of the ggtern package.
I will build an interactive ternary plot using the plot_ly() function of the Plotly R package.

title: Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
2. Installing and Launching R Packages
For this exercise, I will use two main R packages:

ggtern, a ggplot extension specially designed to plot ternary diagrams. The package will be used to plot static ternary plots.
Plotly R, an R package for creating interactive web-based graphs via plotly’s JavaScript graphing library, plotly.js . The plotly R libary contains the ggplotly function, which will convert ggplot2 figures into a Plotly object.

I will also ensure that selected tidyverse family packages — namely readr, dplyr, and tidyr — are installed and loaded.
The code chunk below will accomplish this task.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(plotly, ggtern, tidyverse)

title: Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
3. Data Preparation

3.1 The Data
For this hands-on exercise, I will use the Singapore Residents by Planning AreaSubzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2000-2018 data. The dataset has been downloaded and is stored in the Hands-on W5 sub-folder of my hands-on exercise folder. It is called respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv and is in CSV file format.


3.2 Importing Data
To import respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv into R, I will use the read_csv() function of the readr package.


Show code block
# Reading the data into R environment
pop_data <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W5/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv")




3.3 Preparing the Data
Next, I will use the mutate() function of the dplyr package to derive three new measures: YOUNG, ACTIVE, and OLD.


Show code block
# Deriving the young, economy active and old measures
agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year)) %>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8])) %>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16])) %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018) %>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)

title: Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
4. Plotting Ternary Diagram with R

4.1 Plotting a Static Ternary Diagram
I will use the ggtern() function of the ggtern package to create a simple ternary plot.


Show code block
# Building the static ternary plot
ggtern(data = agpop_mutated, aes(x = YOUNG, y = ACTIVE, z = OLD)) +
  geom_point()









Next, I will enhance the plot by adding a title and applying the theme_rgbw() theme for a cleaner look.


Show code block
# Building the static ternary plot with title and theme
ggtern(data = agpop_mutated, aes(x = YOUNG, y = ACTIVE, z = OLD)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Population structure, 2018") +
  theme_rgbw()











4.2 Plotting an Interactive Ternary Diagram
The code below creates an interactive ternary plot using the plot_ly() function of Plotly R. I first define two reusable helper functions — one for annotations and one for axis formatting — before initiating the visualisation.


Show code block
# Reusable function for creating annotation object
label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt,
    x = 0.1, y = 1,
    ax = 0, ay = 0,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
    align = "center",
    font = list(family = "serif", size = 15, color = "white"),
    bgcolor = "#b3b3b3", bordercolor = "black", borderwidth = 2
  )
}

# Reusable function for axis formatting
axis <- function(txt) {
  list(
    title = txt, tickformat = ".0%", tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"),
  baxis = axis("Active"),
  caxis = axis("Old")
)

# Initiating a plotly visualization
plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated,
  a = ~YOUNG,
  b = ~ACTIVE,
  c = ~OLD,
  color = I("black"),
  type = "scatterternary"
) %>%
  layout(
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes
  )

text:
2. Getting Started

2.1 Installing and loading the packages
For the purpose of this exercise, the following R packages will be used, they are:

title: Visualising Uncertainty
section: 3. Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates: ggplot2 methods
text:
3. Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates: ggplot2 methods
A point estimate is a single number, such as a mean. Uncertainty, on the other hand, is expressed as standard error, confidence interval, or credible interval.






Important



Don’t confuse the uncertainty of a point estimate with the variation in the sample


In this section, I will plot error bars of maths scores by race by using data provided in exam tibble data frame.
Firstly, code chunk below will be used to derive the necessary summary statistics.


Show code block
my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(MATHS),
    sd = sd(MATHS)
  ) %>%
  mutate(se = sd / sqrt(n - 1))








Note



Things to learn from the code chunk above:

group_by() of dplyr package is used to group the observation by RACE,
summarise() is used to compute the count of observations, mean, standard deviation
mutate() is used to derive standard error of Maths by RACE, and
the output is saved as a tibble data table called my_sum.



Next, the code chunk below will be used to display my_sum tibble data frame in an html table format.

3.1 Plotting standard error bars of point estimates
Now we are ready to plot the standard error bars of mean maths score by race as shown below.


Show code block
ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = RACE,
        ymin = mean - se,
        ymax = mean + se),
    width = 0.2,
    colour = "black",
    alpha = 0.9,
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RACE,
                 y = mean),
             stat = "identity",
             color = "red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha = 1) +
  ggtitle("Standard error of mean maths score by race")















Note



Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The error bars are computed by using the formula mean+/-se.
For geom_point(), it is important to indicate stat=“identity”.





3.2 Plotting confidence interval of point estimates
Instead of plotting the standard error bar of point estimates, we can also plot the confidence intervals of mean maths score by race.


Show code block
ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = reorder(RACE, -mean),
        ymin = mean - 1.96 * se,
        ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
    width = 0.2,
    colour = "black",
    alpha = 0.9,
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RACE,
                 y = mean),
             stat = "identity",
             color = "red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha = 1) +
  labs(x = "Maths score",
       title = "95% confidence interval of mean maths score by race")















Note



Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The confidence intervals are computed by using the formula mean+/-1.96*se.
The error bars is sorted by using the average maths scores.
labs() argument of ggplot2 is used to change the x-axis label.





3.3 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates with interactive error bars
In this section, I will plot interactive error bars for the 99% confidence interval of mean maths score by race as shown in the figure below.


Show code block
shared_df = SharedData$new(my_sum)

bscols(widths = c(4, 8),
       ggplotly((ggplot(shared_df) +
                   geom_errorbar(aes(
                     x = reorder(RACE, -mean),
                     ymin = mean - 2.58 * se,
                     ymax = mean + 2.58 * se),
                     width = 0.2,
                     colour = "black",
                     alpha = 0.9,
                     linewidth = 0.5) +
                   geom_point(aes(
                     x = RACE,
                     y = mean,
                     text = paste("Race:", `RACE`,
                                  "<br>N:", `n`,
                                  "<br>Avg. Scores:", round(mean, digits = 2),
                                  "<br>99% CI:[",
                                  round((mean - 2.58 * se), digits = 2), ",",
                                  round((mean + 2.58 * se), digits = 2), "]")),
                     stat = "identity",
                     color = "red",
                     size = 1.5,
                     alpha = 1) +
                   xlab("Race") +
                   ylab("Average Scores") +
                   theme_minimal() +
                   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
                     angle = 45, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
                   ggtitle("99% Confidence interval of average \nmaths scores by race")),
                tooltip = "text"),
       DT::datatable(shared_df,
                     rownames = FALSE,
                     class = "compact",
                     width = "100%",
                     options = list(pageLength = 10,
                                    scrollX = T),
                     colnames = c("No. of pupils",
                                  "Avg Scores",
                                  "Std Dev",
                                  "Std Error")) %>%
         formatRound(columns = c('mean', 'sd', 'se'),
                     digits = 2))

title: Visualising Uncertainty
text:
4. Visualising Uncertainty: ggdist package 

ggdist is an R package that provides a flexible set of ggplot2 geoms and stats designed especially for visualising distributions and uncertainty.
It is designed for both frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty visualization, taking the view that uncertainty visualization can be unified through the perspective of distribution visualization:

for frequentist models, one visualises confidence distributions or bootstrap distributions (see vignette(“freq-uncertainty-vis”));
for Bayesian models, one visualises probability distributions (see the tidybayes package, which builds on top of ggdist).



4.1 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates: ggdist methods
In the code chunk below, stat_pointinterval() of ggdist is used to build a visual for displaying distribution of maths scores by race.


Show code block
exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE,
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of mean math score",
    subtitle = "Mean Point + Multiple-interval plot")















Note



This function comes with many arguments, students are advised to read the syntax reference for more detail.


For example, in the code chunk below the following arguments are used:

.width = 0.95
.point = median
.interval = qi



Show code block
exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(.width = 0.95,
                     .point = median,
                     .interval = qi) +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of median math score",
    subtitle = "Median Point + Multiple-interval plot")











4.2 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates: ggdist methods






Note



The code and plot below will makeover the plot on previous slide by showing 95% and 99% confidence intervals.




Show code block
exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    .width = c(0.95, 0.99),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of mean math score",
    subtitle = "Mean Point + Multiple-interval plot (95% and 99% CI)",
    color = "Confidence Interval"
  )











Show code block
exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, 
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(
    show.legend = FALSE) +   
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of mean math score",
    subtitle = "Mean Point + Multiple-interval plot")















Tip



Gentle advice: This function comes with many arguments, should read the syntax reference for more detail!




4.3 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates: ggdist methods
In the code chunk below, stat_gradientinterval() of ggdist is used to build a visual for displaying distribution of maths scores by race.


Show code block
exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE,
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_gradientinterval(
    fill = "skyblue",
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of mean math score",
    subtitle = "Gradient + interval plot")















Tip



Gentle advice: This function comes with many arguments, should read the syntax reference for more detail!

title: Visualising Distribution
text:
Visualising data distributions isn’t new in statistical analysis. In Chapter 1, I covered some of the most commonly used methods: histograms, probability density curves (PDFs), boxplots, notch plots, and violin plots, and showed how to create them using ggplot2.
In this chapter, I’m introducing two more modern approaches: ridgeline plots and raincloud plots. These techniques offer richer and more intuitive ways to explore distributions, and I’ll walk through how to build them using ggplot2 and its extensions.
