title: Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
Parallel coordinates plot is a data visualisation specially designed for visualising and analysing multivariate, numerical data. It is ideal for comparing multiple variables together and seeing the relationships between them — for example, the variables contributing to the Happiness Index. Parallel coordinates was invented by Alfred Inselberg in the 1970s as a way to visualise high-dimensional data. As pointed out by Stephen Few (2006), this technique’s strength lies in its ability to bring meaningful multivariate patterns and comparisons to light when used interactively for analysis — for example, to characterise clusters detected during customer segmentation.
By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will have gained hands-on experience in:

Plotting static parallel coordinates plots using ggparcoord() of the GGally package, and
Plotting interactive parallel coordinates plots using the parallelPlot package.

text:
2. Installing and Launching R Packages
For this exercise, I will use the GGally, parallelPlot, and tidyverse packages.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(GGally, parallelPlot, tidyverse)

title: Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
3. Data Preparation
In this hands-on exercise, I will use the World Happiness 2018 data. The original data set is in Microsoft Excel format and has been extracted and saved as WHData-2018.csv.
I will use read_csv() of the readr package to import WHData-2018.csv into R and save it as a tibble data frame called wh.


Show code block
wh <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W5/WHData-2018.csv")

title: Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
4. Plotting Static Parallel Coordinates Plot
In this section, I will plot static parallel coordinates plots using ggparcoord() of the GGally package.

4.1 Plotting a Simple Parallel Coordinates
The code chunk below shows the typical syntax to plot a basic static parallel coordinates plot using ggparcoord().


Show code block
ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12))









Only two arguments are used: data maps the data object (wh), and columns selects the columns for the plot.


4.2 Plotting a Parallel Coordinates with Boxplot
The basic parallel coordinates failed to reveal meaningful insights into the World Happiness measures. I will now improve the plot using a collection of arguments provided by ggparcoord().


Show code block
ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Variables")









Things to note:

groupColumn groups the parallel lines by a single variable (Region) and colours them by region name.
scale = "uniminmax" univariately scales each variable so the minimum is 0 and the maximum is 1.
alphaLines = 0.2 reduces the intensity of the line colour. Permissible range is 0 to 1.
boxplot = TRUE turns on the boxplot overlay.
title provides the plot a title.



4.3 Parallel Coordinates with Facet
Since ggparcoord() is built on ggplot2, I can combine it with ggplot2 functions. Below I use facet_wrap() to plot 10 small multiple parallel coordinates plots — one per geographical region.


Show code block
ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)









One aesthetic issue is that some variable names overlap on the x-axis.


4.4 Rotating x-axis Text Label
To make the x-axis text labels easier to read, I will rotate them by 30 degrees using theme().


Show code block
ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))









axis.text.x is passed to theme() with element_text(angle = 30) to rotate x-axis text by 30 degrees.


4.5 Adjusting the Rotated x-axis Text Label
Rotating to 30 degrees may cause labels to overlap with the plot. I can avoid this by adjusting the text location using hjust within element_text().


Show code block
ggparcoord(data = wh,
           columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

title: Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
section: 5. Plotting Interactive Parallel Coordinates Plot: parallelPlot Methods
text:
5. Plotting Interactive Parallel Coordinates Plot: parallelPlot Methods
parallelPlot is an R package specially designed to plot parallel coordinates plots using the htmlwidgets package and d3.js. In this section, I will use functions provided in parallelPlot to build interactive parallel coordinates plots.

5.1 The Basic Plot
The code chunk below plots an interactive parallel coordinates plot using parallelPlot().


Show code block
wh <- wh %>%
  select("Happiness score", c(7:12))
parallelPlot(wh,
             width = 320,
             height = 250)






Some axis labels may be too long. I will address this in the next step.


5.2 Rotate Axis Label
I use the rotateTitle argument to avoid overlapping axis labels.


Show code block
parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE)






One useful interactive feature of parallelPlot is that clicking on a variable of interest (e.g. Happiness score) changes the colour scheme from a monotonous blue to blues with varying intensity.


5.3 Changing the Colour Scheme
I can change the default blue colour scheme using the continuousCS argument.


Show code block
parallelPlot(wh,
             continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
             rotateTitle = TRUE)








5.4 Parallel Coordinates Plot with Histogram
Using the histoVisibility argument, I can plot a histogram along the axis of each variable.


Show code block
histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh))
parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisibility)

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
1. Overview
In this hands-on exercise, I will learn how to model, analyse and visualise network data using R. By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will be able to:

create graph object data frames, manipulate them using appropriate functions of dplyr, lubridate, and tidygraph,
build network graph visualisations using appropriate functions of ggraph,
compute network geometrics using tidygraph,
build advanced graph visualisations by incorporating network geometrics, and
build interactive network visualisations using the visNetwork package.

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
2. Getting Started

Installing and loading the packagesThe data


For this exercise, four network data modelling and visualisation packages will be installed and launched: igraph, tidygraph, ggraph, and visNetwork. Beside these, tidyverse, lubridate, graphlayouts, concaveman, and ggforce will also be installed and loaded.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(igraph, tidygraph, ggraph,
               visNetwork, lubridate, clock,
               tidyverse, graphlayouts,
               concaveman, ggforce)




The datasets used in this exercise are from an oil exploration and extraction company. There are two datasets:

GAStech-email_edges.csv - contains two weeks of 9,063 email correspondences between 55 employees.
GAStech_email_nodes.csv - contains the names, departments, and titles of the 55 employees.

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
3. The Data

3.1 Importing Network Data from Files
I will import GAStech_email_node.csv and GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv into R using read_csv() of the readr package.


Show code block
GAStech_nodes <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W7/GAStech_email_node.csv")
GAStech_edges <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W7/GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv")




3.2 Reviewing the Imported Data
I will examine the structure of the edges data frame using glimpse() of dplyr.


Show code block
glimpse(GAStech_edges)


Rows: 9,063
Columns: 8
$ source      <dbl> 43, 43, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 26, 26, 26…
$ target      <dbl> 41, 40, 51, 52, 53, 45, 44, 46, 48, 49, 47, 54, 27, 28, 29…
$ SentDate    <chr> "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014"…
$ SentTime    <time> 08:39:00, 08:39:00, 08:58:00, 08:58:00, 08:58:00, 08:58:0…
$ Subject     <chr> "GT-SeismicProcessorPro Bug Report", "GT-SeismicProcessorP…
$ MainSubject <chr> "Work related", "Work related", "Work related", "Work rela…
$ sourceLabel <chr> "Sven.Flecha", "Sven.Flecha", "Kanon.Herrero", "Kanon.Herr…
$ targetLabel <chr> "Isak.Baza", "Lucas.Alcazar", "Felix.Resumir", "Hideki.Coc…








Warning



The output above reveals that SentDate is treated as a Character data type instead of a Date data type. This is an error! I need to change the data type of SentDate back to Date before continuing.




3.3 Wrangling Time
The code chunk below converts SentDate to proper Date format and adds a Weekday field.


Show code block
GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(SentDate,
                        label = TRUE,
                        abbr = FALSE))








NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




Both dmy() and wday() are functions of the lubridate package, which makes it easier to work with dates and times.
dmy() transforms the SentDate field to Date data type.
wday() returns the day of the week as a decimal number or an ordered factor if label = TRUE. With abbr = FALSE, day names are spelt in full (e.g., Monday). The result is stored in the new Weekday column.
The values in the Weekday field are in ordinal scale.





3.4 Reviewing the Revised Date Fields


Show code block
glimpse(GAStech_edges)


Rows: 9,063
Columns: 10
$ source      <dbl> 43, 43, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 44, 26, 26, 26…
$ target      <dbl> 41, 40, 51, 52, 53, 45, 44, 46, 48, 49, 47, 54, 27, 28, 29…
$ SentDate    <chr> "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014", "6/1/2014"…
$ SentTime    <time> 08:39:00, 08:39:00, 08:58:00, 08:58:00, 08:58:00, 08:58:0…
$ Subject     <chr> "GT-SeismicProcessorPro Bug Report", "GT-SeismicProcessorP…
$ MainSubject <chr> "Work related", "Work related", "Work related", "Work rela…
$ sourceLabel <chr> "Sven.Flecha", "Sven.Flecha", "Kanon.Herrero", "Kanon.Herr…
$ targetLabel <chr> "Isak.Baza", "Lucas.Alcazar", "Felix.Resumir", "Hideki.Coc…
$ SendDate    <date> 2014-01-06, 2014-01-06, 2014-01-06, 2014-01-06, 2014-01-0…
$ Weekday     <ord> Friday, Friday, Friday, Friday, Friday, Friday, Friday, Fr…




3.5 Wrangling Attributes
The edges data frame currently consists of individual email flow records, which is not ideal for visualisation. I will aggregate the records by source, target, and day of the week, then compute a Weight field.


Show code block
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
    summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source!=target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()








NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




Four functions from the dplyr package are used: filter(), group_by(), summarise(), and ungroup().
The output data frame is called GAStech_edges_aggregated.
A new field called Weight has been added, representing the number of emails sent between each pair on a given weekday.





3.6 Reviewing the Revised Edges File


Show code block
glimpse(GAStech_edges_aggregated)


Rows: 1,372
Columns: 4

$ Weekday <ord> Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Sunday, Monday, Tu…

4. Creating Network Objects Using tidygraph
In this section, I will create a graph data model using the tidygraph package. It provides a tidy API for graph/network manipulation by representing network data as two tidy tables - one for nodes and one for edges - and allows switching between them using dplyr verbs.

4.1 Using tbl_graph() to Build the tidygraph Data Model
I will use tbl_graph() of the tidygraph package to build a network graph data frame.


Show code block
GAStech_graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = GAStech_nodes,
                           edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated,
                           directed = TRUE)




4.2 Reviewing the Output tidygraph Object

The Node Data is marked as active. The notion of an active tibble within a tbl_graph object makes it possible to manipulate one tibble at a time.

The nodes tibble is activated by default. I can switch the active tibble using activate(). For example, to rearrange rows in the edges tibble by descending Weight:

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
section: 5. Plotting Static Network Graphs with ggraph
text:
5. Plotting Static Network Graphs with ggraph
ggraph is an extension of ggplot2, making it easier to carry over basic ggplot skills to network graph design. Every ggraph network graph has three main aspects: nodes, edges, and layouts.

5.1 Plotting a Basic Network Graph
The code chunk below uses ggraph(), geom_edge_link(), and geom_node_point() to plot a basic network graph.


Show code block
ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




The basic plotting function is ggraph(), which takes the data and the desired layout type. It can accept either an igraph object or a tbl_graph object.





5.2 Changing the Default Network Graph Theme
I will use theme_graph() to remove the x and y axes for a cleaner look.


Show code block
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




theme_graph() removes axes, grids, and borders, and changes the font to Arial Narrow.
The ggraph theme can be set for a series of plots using set_graph_style() before plotting, or applied per plot using theme_graph().





5.3 Changing the Colouring of the Plot
theme_graph() also makes it easy to change the overall colour scheme of the plot.


Show code block
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = 'grey50')) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = 'grey40'))

g + theme_graph(background = 'grey10',
                text_colour = 'white')











5.4 Working with ggraph’s layouts
ggraph support many layout for standard used, they are: star, circle, nicely (default), dh, gem, graphopt, grid, mds, spahere, randomly, fr, kk, drl and lgl. Figures below and on the right show layouts supported by ggraph().



5.5 Fruchterman and Reingold Layout
The code chunk below plots the network graph using the Fruchterman and Reingold layout by setting layout = "fr".


Show code block
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




The layout argument defines the layout algorithm to use. ggraph supports many layouts including: star, circle, nicely, dh, gem, graphopt, grid, mds, randomly, fr, kk, drl and lgl.





5.5 Modifying Network Nodes
I will colour each node by its respective department.


Show code block
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = 3))

g + theme_graph()















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




geom_node_point() is equivalent in functionality to geom_point() of ggplot2. It allows for simple plotting of nodes in different shapes, colours and sizes.





5.6 Modifying Edges
I will map the edge thickness to the Weight variable to show email volume.


Show code block
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 3)

g + theme_graph()















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




geom_edge_link() draws edges as straight lines between start and end nodes. The width argument maps line width proportionally to the Weight attribute, and alpha introduces opacity.

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
6. Creating Facet Graphs
Faceting is a very useful feature in ggraph to reduce edge over-plotting by spreading nodes and edges out based on their attributes. There are three faceting functions:

facet_nodes() - edges are only drawn in a panel if both terminal nodes are present.
facet_edges() - nodes are always drawn in all panels.
facet_graph() - facets on two variables simultaneously.


6.1 Working with facet_edges()


Show code block
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)











6.2 Working with facet_edges() - Moving the Legend
I will use theme() to move the legend to the bottom.


Show code block
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

g + facet_edges(~Weekday)











6.3 A Framed Facet Graph
I will use th_foreground() to add a frame border around each facet panel.


Show code block
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~Weekday) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",
                border = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')











6.4 Working with facet_nodes()


Show code block
set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph,
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department),
                  size = 2)

g + facet_nodes(~Department)+
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",
                border = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
text:
7. Network Metrics Analysis

7.1 Computing Centrality Indices
Centrality measures describe the relative importance of actors in a network. There are four well-known measures: degree, betweenness, closeness, and eigenvector.
I will use centrality_betweenness() of tidygraph to compute betweenness centrality and map it to node size.


Show code block
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
            size=betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph()











7.2 Visualising Network Metrics
The code below computes centrality directly inside the aes() call.


Show code block
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()











7.3 Visualising Community
I will use group_edge_betweenness() to detect communities and colour nodes accordingly.


Show code block
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      width=Weight),
    alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()









I will now enhance the community visualisation by adding convex hull boundaries around each community using geom_mark_hull() of the ggforce package, and using group_optimal() for community detection.


Show code block
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y,
        group = community,
        fill = community),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight),
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                      size = betweenness_measure),
                      color = "black",
                      shape = 21)

g + theme_graph()

title: Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R
section: 8. Building Interactive Network Graph with visNetwork
text:
8. Building Interactive Network Graph with visNetwork
visNetwork uses a nodes list and edges list to create an interactive network. The nodes list must include an id column, and the edges list must have from and to columns.

8.1 Data Preparation
I will prepare the edges data to use from and to columns (required by visNetwork) by joining with the nodes data.


Show code block
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
    summarise(weight = n()) %>%
  filter(from!=to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()




8.2 Plotting the First Interactive Network Graph


Show code block
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated)








8.3 Working with Layout
I will use visIgraphLayout() to apply the Fruchterman-Reingold layout.


Show code block
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr")








8.4 Working with Visual Attributes - Nodes
visNetwork looks for a group column in the nodes data frame to colour nodes automatically. I will rename Department to group.


Show code block
GAStech_nodes <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  rename(group = Department)


I will now re-plot with the legend added.


Show code block
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)








8.5 Working with Visual Attributes - Edges
I will use visEdges() to add directional arrows and curved edges.


Show code block
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to",
           smooth = list(enabled = TRUE,
                         type = "curvedCW")) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)








8.6 Interactivity
I will use visOptions() to add interactive features: highlighting nearest nodes and a node ID selection dropdown.


Show code block
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE,
             nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
1. Learning Outcome
By the end of this hands-on exercise I will be able to create the following data visualisations by using R packages:

plotting a calendar heatmap by using ggplot2 functions,
plotting a cycle plot by using ggplot2 function,
plotting a slopegraph, and
plotting a horizon chart.

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
2. Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading R Packages
Write a code chunk to check, install and launch the following R packages: scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes, gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table, CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, and tidyverse.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
3. Plotting Calendar Heatmap
In this section, I will learn how to plot a calendar heatmap programmatically by using the ggplot2 package.
By the end of this section, I will be able to:

plot a calendar heatmap by using ggplot2 functions and extension,
write a function using R programming,
derive specific date and time related fields by using base R and lubridate packages, and
perform data preparation tasks by using tidyr and dplyr packages.


3.1 The Data
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, eventlog.csv will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.


3.2 Importing the Data
First, I will use the code chunk below to import eventlog.csv into R environment and call the data frame as attacks.


Show code block
attacks <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W8/eventlog.csv")




3.3 Examining the Data Structure
It is always a good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed.
For example, kable() can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.


Show code block
kable(head(attacks))

source_country
tz

Note



There are three columns, namely timestamp, source_country and tz.

timestamp field stores date-time values in POSIXct format.
source_country field stores the source of the attack. It is in ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code.
tz field stores the time zone of the source IP address.





3.4 Data Preparation
Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour of day fields
Before we can plot the calendar heatmap, two new fields namely wkday and hour need to be derived. In this step, I will write a function to perform the task.


Show code block
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts,
                        tz = tz[1],
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}








Note




ymd_hms() and hour() are from the lubridate package, and
weekdays() is a base R function.



Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame


Show code block
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday',
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday',
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))








Note



Beside extracting the necessary data into the attacks data frame, mutate() of the dplyr package is used to convert wkday and hour fields into factor so they’ll be ordered when plotting.


The table below shows the tidy tibble table after processing.


Show code block
kable(head(attacks))

3.5 Building the Calendar Heatmap


Show code block
grouped <- attacks %>%
  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
            size = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue",
                      high = "dark blue") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6))















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




A tibble data table called grouped is derived by aggregating the attack by wkday and hour fields.
A new field called n is derived by using group_by() and count() functions.
na.omit() is used to exclude missing values.
geom_tile() is used to plot tiles (grids) at each x and y position. The color and size arguments are used to specify the border colour and line size of the tiles.
theme_tufte() of the ggthemes package is used to remove unnecessary chart junk. To learn which visual components of default ggplot2 have been excluded, you are encouraged to comment out this line to examine the default plot.
coord_equal() is used to ensure the plot will have an aspect ratio of 1:1.
scale_fill_gradient() function is used to create a two colour gradient (low–high).



Then I can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it. Since there are values for every combination, there is no need to further preprocess the data.


3.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Challenge: Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.
Step 1: Deriving attack by country object
In order to identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, I am required to:

count the number of attacks by country,
calculate the percent of attacks by country, and
save the results in a tibble data frame.



Show code block
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))


Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame
In this step, I will extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from the attacks data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame called top4_attacks.


Show code block
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()


Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calendar Heatmap by using ggplot2 package.


Show code block
ggplot(top4_attacks,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
            size = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue",
                      high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6))

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
4. Plotting Cycle Plot
In this section, I will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.

4.1 Step 1: Data Import
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, arrivals_by_air.xlsx will be used.
The code chunk below imports arrivals_by_air.xlsx by using read_excel() of the readxl package and saves it as a tibble data frame called air.


Show code block
air <- read_excel("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W8/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")




4.2 Step 2: Deriving Month and Year Fields
Next, two new fields called month and year are derived from the Month-Year field.


Show code block
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`),
                    levels=1:12,
                    labels=month.abb,
                    ordered=TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))




4.3 Step 4: Extracting the Target Country
Next, the code chunk below is used to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam).


Show code block
Vietnam <- air %>%
  select(`Vietnam`,
         month,
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)




4.4 Step 5: Computing Year Average Arrivals by Month
The code chunk below uses group_by() and summarise() of dplyr to compute year average arrivals by month.


Show code block
hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))




4.5 Step 6: Plotting the Cycle Plot
The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot.


Show code block
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year,
                y=`Vietnam`,
                group=month),
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue),
             data=hline.data,
             linetype=6,
             colour="red",
             size=0.5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

title: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
5. Plotting Slopegraph
In this section I will learn how to plot a slopegraph by using R.
Before getting started, I will note that the original chapter uses newggslopegraph() from the CGPfunctions package. Since that package is no longer available on CRAN, I will build the slopegraph using ggplot2 directly to achieve the same result.

5.1 Step 1: Data Import
Import the rice data set into R environment by using the code chunk below.


Show code block
rice <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W8/rice.csv")




5.2 Step 2: Plotting the Slopegraph
The code chunk below is used to plot a basic slopegraph comparing rice yields across top Asian countries between 1961 and 1980.


Show code block
rice_slope <- rice %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year))

ggplot(data = rice_slope,
       aes(x = Year,
           y = Yield,
           group = Country)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = Country),
            linewidth = 0.75,
            alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Country),
             size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = rice_slope %>% filter(Year == 1961),
            aes(label = Country, color = Country),
            hjust = 1.15,
            size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = rice_slope %>% filter(Year == 1980),
            aes(label = Country, color = Country),
            hjust = -0.15,
            size = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(mult = 0.35)) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.ticks = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
       subtitle = "1961-1980",
       caption = "Prepared by: Do Thi Tue Minh",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Yield (tonnes/ha)")















NoteThing to learn from the code chunk above



For effective data visualisation design, factor() is used to convert the value type of the Year field from numeric to factor.

title: Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
1. Learning Outcome
By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will be able to:

import an aspatial data file into R,
convert it into a simple point feature data frame by using the appropriate coordinate system, and
plot interactive proportional symbol maps using the tmap package.

title: Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
2. Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading R Packages
The R packages required for this exercise are: sf, tmap, and tidyverse. The code chunk below uses pacman::p_load() to check, install, and load all the necessary packages.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)

title: Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
3. Geospatial Data Wrangling

3.1 The Data
The data set used in this hands-on exercise is SGPools_svy21.csv. It is a csv file that consists of 306 observations and 7 variables. The seven variables are: NAME, ADDRESS, POSTCODE, XCOORD, YCOORD, OUTLET TYPE, and Gp1Gp2 Winnings. The XCOORD and YCOORD columns are in the Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System (EPSG: 3414).
Figure below shows the first 15 records of SGPools_svy21.csv. It consists of seven columns. The XCOORD and YCOORD columns are the x-coordinates and y-coordinates of SingPools outlets and branches. They are in Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinates System.



3.2 Importing the Data
The code chunk below uses read_csv() of the readr package to import SGPools_svy21.csv into R as a tibble data frame called sgpools.


Show code block
sgpools <- read_csv("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W9/SGPools_svy21.csv")


After importing the data file, it is important to examine whether the data has been imported correctly.


Show code block

Notice that the sgpools data in tibble data frame format contains 306 rows and 7 columns. The XCOORD and YCOORD are currently stored as numeric values and therefore not yet recognised as geographic coordinates.


3.3 Creating a Simple Feature Data Frame from an Aspatial Data Frame
The code chunk below converts sgpools into a simple feature data frame by using st_as_sf() of the sf package.


Show code block
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs = 3414)








Note




The coords argument requires the column name of the x-coordinates first, followed by the column name of the y-coordinates.
The crs argument requires the coordinates system in EPSG format. EPSG: 3414 is the Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System. You can search for other countries’ EPSG codes at epsg.io.



Figure below shows the data table of sgpools_sf. Notice that a new column called geometry has been added into the data frame.

title: Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
4. Drawing Proportional Symbol Maps
To create an interactive proportional symbol map in R, the view mode of tmap will be used.
The code chunk below turns on the interactive mode of tmap.


Show code block
tmap_mode("view")



4.1 Creating an Interactive Point Symbol Map
The code chunk below is used to create an interactive point symbol map.


Show code block
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)








4.2 Making the Proportional Symbol Map
To draw a proportional symbol map, I need to assign a numerical variable to the size argument of tm_bubbles(). The size of each bubble will then be proportional to the value of the selected variable.


Show code block
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)













Note



It is easy to see that the larger the Gp1Gp2 Winnings amount, the bigger the bubble on the map.




4.3 Using Fill to Differentiate Between Outlet Types
The fill argument can be used to encode a categorical variable with colour. In the code chunk below, OUTLET TYPE is mapped to fill to differentiate between branch types.


Show code block
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)










4.4 Synchronised Small Multiple Maps with tm_facets()
An impressive and useful feature of tmap is that it allows a faceted map to be created in view mode, whereby the coordinated view is enabled by default. The sync argument in tm_facets() is used to produce multiple maps with synchronised zoom and pan settings.


Show code block
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_facets(by = "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)























Note



Before creating the faceted map shown above, tmap_mode("view") must be called to activate the interactive viewing mode.


The code chunk below switches tmap back to the static plot mode.


Show code block
tmap_mode("plot")

title: Information Dashboard Design with R
text:
1. Learning Outcome
By the end of this hands-on exercise, I will be able to:

create bullet charts using ggplot2,
create sparklines using ggplot2,
build a static information dashboard by using gt and gtExtras, and
build an interactive information dashboard by using reactable and reactablefmtr.

title: Information Dashboard Design with R
text:
2. Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading R Packages
The R packages required for this exercise are: lubridate, ggthemes, reactable, reactablefmtr, gt, gtExtras, and tidyverse. The code chunk below uses pacman::p_load() to check, install, and load all the necessary packages.


Show code block
pacman::p_load(lubridate, ggthemes, reactable,
               reactablefmtr, gt, gtExtras, tidyverse, dataui)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

title: Information Dashboard Design with R
text:
3. Importing Microsoft Access Database

3.1 The Data Set
The data set used in this hands-on exercise is the Coffee Chain Microsoft Access database (Coffee Chain.mdb). It contains transactional sales data for a coffee chain, including product names, sales figures, budget targets, and dates.


3.2 Importing the Database into R






Note



The code below uses the RODBC package to connect to the Microsoft Access database. This approach only works on Windows with a compatible 32-bit ODBC driver. On macOS, this step is not available — I will load the pre-exported CoffeeChain.rds file directly instead (see the next code chunk).




Show code block
library(RODBC)
con <- odbcConnectAccess2007('Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W10/Coffee Chain.mdb')
coffeechain <- sqlFetch(con, 'CoffeeChain Query')
write_rds(coffeechain, "Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W10/CoffeeChain.rds")
odbcClose(con)


Since I am working on macOS, I will load the data directly from the pre-exported RDS file.


Show code block
coffeechain <- read_rds("Hands-on Exercises/Hands-on W10/CoffeeChain.rds")




3.3 Data Preparation
The code chunk below aggregates the data at the product level, deriving the total budget sales (target) and actual sales (current) for each product.


Show code block
product <- coffeechain %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `current` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup()




3.4 Bullet Chart in ggplot2
A bullet chart is a variation of a bar chart designed to replace dashboard gauges and meters. It compares an actual value against a target and shows qualitative performance ranges (e.g. poor, satisfactory, good) in the background.


Show code block
ggplot(product, aes(Product, current)) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, max(target) * 1.01),
           fill = "grey85", width = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.75),
           fill = "grey60", width = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.5),
           fill = "grey50", width = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, current),
           width = 0.35,
           fill = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(y = target,
                    x = Product,
                    ymin = target,
                    ymax = target),
                width = 0.4,
                colour = "red",
                size = 1) +
  coord_flip()















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




Three background bars of decreasing shade (grey85 → grey60 → grey50) represent qualitative performance bands — here set at 100%, 75%, and 50% of the target.
The narrow black bar represents actual current sales.
geom_errorbar() with ymin = ymax = target draws a single horizontal line marking the target value.
coord_flip() rotates the chart so products appear on the y-axis, making it easier to read long product names.

title: Information Dashboard Design with R
text:
4. Plotting Sparklines Using ggplot2
A sparkline is a small, condensed line chart without axes or labels that shows a trend at a glance. They are often placed alongside data tables to give context to summary statistics.

4.1 Preparing the Data
The code chunk below filters the data to 2013, derives a Month field, and aggregates sales by month and product.


Show code block
sales_report <- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  mutate(Month = month(Date)) %>%
  group_by(Month, Product) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Month, Product, Sales)


Next, I compute the minimum and maximum sales months, the end-of-period values, and the interquartile range for each product — all of which will be used to annotate the sparklines.


Show code block
mins <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.min(Sales))

maxs <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.max(Sales))

ends <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  filter(Month == max(Month))

quarts <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(quart1 = quantile(Sales, 0.25),
            quart2 = quantile(Sales, 0.75)) %>%
  right_join(sales_report)




4.2 Sparklines in ggplot2
The code chunk below uses facet_grid() to produce one sparkline per product, with an IQR ribbon, annotated min/max points, and end-of-period labels.


Show code block
ggplot(sales_report, aes(x = Month, y = Sales)) +
  facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_ribbon(data = quarts,
              aes(ymin = quart1, max = quart2),
              fill = "grey90") +
  geom_line(size = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = mins, col = "red") +
  geom_point(data = maxs, col = "blue") +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.0) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) +
                  (0.25 * (max(sales_report$Month) - min(sales_report$Month)))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 12, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  theme_tufte(base_size = 3, base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_blank())















NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") creates one panel per product with independent y-axis scales, so small-sales products are still readable.
The grey ribbon from geom_ribbon() visualises the interquartile range (Q1 to Q3) as a band of typical performance.
Red points mark monthly sales lows; blue points mark highs.
expand_limits() adds extra space on the right so the product name labels are not clipped.
theme_tufte() strips away all chart junk, keeping only the data elements.

6.1 Plotting Coffeechain Sales Report
To use gt_plt_sparkline(), the monthly sales values must first be stored as a list column — one list of values per product row.

  mutate(Year = year(Date)) %>%
  filter(Year == "2013") %>%

                       label = TRUE,

  group_by(Product, Month) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup()


The code chunk below converts the monthly sales into a list column.

title: Information Dashboard Design with R
section: 7. Interactive Information Dashboard: reactable and reactablefmtr Methods
text:
7. Interactive Information Dashboard: reactable and reactablefmtr Methods
The reactable and reactablefmtr packages allow the creation of interactive HTML tables with embedded charts. The react_sparkline() function requires the dataui package, which must be installed from GitHub.


Show code block
remotes::install_github("timelyportfolio/dataui")


First, I will reshape the report data into the list-column format required by reactablefmtr.


Show code block
report <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize(`Monthly Sales` = list(Sales))



7.1 Plotting Interactive Sparklines


Show code block
reactable(
  report,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)








7.2 Changing the Page Size
By default, reactable shows 10 rows per page. Since there are 13 products, I will set defaultPageSize = 13 to display all of them at once.


Show code block
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)








7.3 Adding Points and Labels
The code chunk below highlights the minimum and maximum sales months with coloured points and adds first/last value labels.


Show code block
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        labels = c("first", "last")
      )
    )
  )
)








7.4 Adding a Reference Line
The code chunk below adds a mean reference line to each sparkline, making it easy to see which months were above or below average.


Show code block
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        statline = "mean"
      )
    )
  )
)








7.5 Adding a Bandline
The code chunk below adds an interquartile range band (Q1 to Q3) in green, providing a visual reference for the typical range of monthly sales.


Show code block
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        line_width = 1,
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        bandline_color = "green"
      )
    )
  )
)








7.6 Changing from Sparkline to Sparkbar
Instead of a line chart, I can use react_sparkbar() to render each product’s monthly trend as a bar chart.


Show code block
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkbar(
        report,
        highlight_bars = highlight_bars(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        statline = "mean"
      )
    )
  )
)












NoteThings to learn from the code chunk




react_sparkbar() replaces react_sparkline() to render bars instead of a line.
highlight_bars() colours the minimum month red and the maximum month blue, mirroring the point highlighting used in the sparkline version.
Combining bandline and statline gives readers both a typical-range band and a mean reference at a glance.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Visual Analytics Report
text:
This technical report applies visual analytics techniques to a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset from a Spanish non-life insurer (sourced from Mendeley Data). The dataset contains approximately 354,000 policy-year records spanning 2022-2024.
The two primary analytical objectives are:

Univariate analysis: Explore the distributions and characteristics of numerical and categorical variables across the portfolio.
Bivariate analysis: Investigate and statistically validate factors that influence portfolio profitability (loss ratio) and volatility (claim frequency and severity).

2. Data Preparation

2.1 Approach
Before analysis, three preparatory steps were applied to the raw data:

Type conversion: Several variables are stored as numeric codes in the source file and were recoded as ordered or nominal factors with descriptive labels to support meaningful visualisation.
Feature engineering: 3 key actuarial performance metrics (loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity) will be derived.
Missing value assessment



2.2. Loading Packages

  DT,           # interactive HTML tables
  broom,         # tidy statistical test outputs

)

dict_path <- "Take Home 1/A detailed dataset of motor insurance policies wit/Descriptive of variables.xlsx"

2.6 Reproducibility and Data Quality Checks
The source is a policy-year file, so a record should be uniquely identified by insured_id and year. The checks below verify row uniqueness, exposure bounds, missingness concentration, and whether the component premium and incurred fields reconcile closely with their totals.


Show code block
premium_components <- c(
  "liability_premium", "property_damage_premium", "theft_premium",
  "fire_premium", "glass_premium", "legal_protection_premium",
  "occupants_premium"
)

incurred_components <- c(
  "liability_incurred", "property_incurred", "theft_incurred",
  "fire_incurred", "glass_incurred", "legal_protection_incurred",
  "occupants_incurred"
)

dq_checks <- tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Policy-year duplicate records",
    "Rows with exposure outside [0, 1]",
    "Rows with non-positive total premium",
    "Rows with missing vehicle value",
    "Rows where premium components do not reconcile",
    "Rows where incurred components do not reconcile"
  ),
  Count = c(
    motor_raw |> count(insured_id, year) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow(),
    motor_raw |> filter(total_exposure < 0 | total_exposure > 1) |> nrow(),
    motor_raw |> filter(total_premium <= 0) |> nrow(),
    sum(is.na(motor_raw$vehicle_value)),
    motor_raw |>
      mutate(component_premium = rowSums(across(all_of(premium_components)), na.rm = TRUE),
             diff = abs(total_premium - component_premium)) |>
      filter(diff > 0.01) |>
      nrow(),
    motor_raw |>
      mutate(component_incurred = rowSums(across(all_of(incurred_components)), na.rm = TRUE),
             diff = abs(total_incurred - component_incurred)) |>
      filter(diff > 0.01) |>
      nrow()
  )
) |>
  mutate(`Share of Rows` = percent(Count / nrow(motor_raw), 0.001))

2.7 Data Wrangling
Character columns are converted to factors with descriptive labels matching the data dictionary. bonus_score is declared as ordered (Good > Neutral > Bad) because it represents a ranked risk tier used in actuarial pricing.


Show code block
motor <- motor_raw |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),

    policy_type = factor(
      policy_type,
      levels = c("TP", "TPG", "CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N")
    ),

    policy_status = factor(
      policy_status,
      levels = c("A", "C"),
      labels = c("Active", "Cancelled")
    ),

    business_type = factor(
      business_type,
      levels = c("NB", "P"),
      labels = c("New Business", "Portfolio")
    ),

    payment_frequency = factor(
      payment_frequency,
      levels = c("A", "S", "Q"),
      labels = c("Annual", "Semiannual", "Quarterly")
    ),

    bonus_score = factor(
      bonus_score,
      levels  = c("G", "N", "B"),
      labels  = c("Good", "Neutral", "Bad"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),

    fuel_type = factor(
      fuel_type,
      levels = c("G", "D"),
      labels = c("Gasoline", "Diesel")
    ),

    municipality_type = factor(
      municipality_type,
      levels = c("I", "C", "IS"),
      labels = c("Inland", "Coastal", "Islands")
    ),

    circulation_area = factor(
      circulation_area,
      levels = c("U", "R"),
      labels = c("Urban", "Rural")
    ),

    vehicle_brand = str_to_title(vehicle_brand)
  )




2.8 Feature Engineering
Three core actuarial metrics and two derived grouping variables are created:








Metric
Formula
Purpose




Loss Ratio
total_incurred / total_premium
Profitability — values > 1 indicate underwriting losses


Claim Frequency
total_claims / total_exposure
How often claims occur per unit of exposure


Claim Severity
total_incurred / total_claims
Average cost per claim (only for policies with ≥1 claim)


Driving Experience
year − age_driving_licence
Years since the driver obtained their licence


Age Bands
cut() on driver_age / vehicle_age
Discretised groups for segment-level analysis





Show code block
motor <- motor |>
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = if_else(total_premium > 0,
                         total_incurred / total_premium,
                         NA_real_),

    claim_freq = if_else(total_exposure > 0,
                         total_claims / total_exposure,
                         NA_real_),

    claim_sev  = if_else(total_claims > 0,
                         total_incurred / total_claims,
                         NA_real_),

    has_claim  = total_claims > 0,

    driving_exp = as.integer(as.character(year)) - age_driving_licence,

    driver_age_band = cut(
      driver_age,
      breaks = c(17, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, Inf),
      labels = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-45", "46-55", "56-65", "65+"),
      right  = TRUE
    ),

    vehicle_age_band = cut(
      vehicle_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 2, 5, 10, 15, Inf),
      labels = c("0-2", "3-5", "6-10", "11-15", "15+")
    )
  )

Show code block

  summarise(
    `Total Policy-Years`       = comma(n()),
    `Unique Insureds`          = comma(n_distinct(insured_id)),
    `Years Covered`            = paste(levels(year), collapse = ", "),
    `Active Policies`          = percent(mean(policy_status == "Active"), 0.1),
    `Policies with Claims`     = percent(mean(has_claim), 0.1),
    `Mean Loss Ratio`          = as.character(round(mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE), 4)),
    `Aggregate Loss Ratio`     = as.character(round(sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium), 4)),
    `Mean Total Premium (EUR)` = comma(round(mean(total_premium), 2))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Metric", values_to = "Value") |>

2.10 Premium and Loss Component Sandbox
The portfolio has multiple coverage components. Before analysing overall loss ratio, the component view below checks which coverages contribute most to written premium and incurred losses. This is useful because volatility may be concentrated in one claim type even when aggregate portfolio profitability appears acceptable.


Show code block
component_long <- motor |>
  transmute(
    year,
    Liability = liability_premium,
    Property = property_damage_premium,
    Theft = theft_premium,
    Fire = fire_premium,
    Glass = glass_premium,
    Legal = legal_protection_premium,
    Occupants = occupants_premium,
    Liability_incurred = liability_incurred,
    Property_incurred = property_incurred,
    Theft_incurred = theft_incurred,
    Fire_incurred = fire_incurred,
    Glass_incurred = glass_incurred,
    Legal_incurred = legal_protection_incurred,
    Occupants_incurred = occupants_incurred
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -year,
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "amount"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = if_else(str_detect(component, "_incurred$"), "Incurred Loss", "Premium"),
    component = component |>
      str_remove("_incurred$") |>
      str_replace_all("_", " ") |>
      str_to_title()
  )

component_summary <- component_long |>
  group_by(year, measure, component) |>
  summarise(amount = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(year, measure) |>
  mutate(share = amount / sum(amount)) |>
  ungroup()




Show code block
component_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = share, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~measure) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3", name = "Coverage Component") +
  labs(
    title = "Portfolio Composition by Coverage Component",
    subtitle = "Comparing premium share with incurred-loss share identifies whether pricing and loss emergence are aligned",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of Annual Total"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")





Premium and incurred-loss composition by year




Interpretation:

Liability and property dominate both premium and incurred losses, with the loss-side mix showing slightly more year-on-year variation than the premium side. This suggests aggregate loss ratios may mask component-level differences, motivating a closer examination of frequency and severity by coverage type.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Visual Analytics Report
text:
3. Univariate Visual Analytics
This section examines each variable individually to understand the portfolio’s composition: the mix of coverage types, driver profiles, vehicle characteristics, and geographic spread, before moving to inter-variable comparisons.

3.1 Categorical Variables

3.1.1 Policy and Insured Characteristics
Policy type is a nominal variable, so a sorted horizontal bar chart is used to compare category size directly while keeping the policy labels readable.


Show code block
motor |>
  count(policy_type) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(policy_type, n), y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct, 0.1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Policy Types",
    subtitle = "CC and COMP_E (comprehensive with excess) account for the majority of the portfolio",
    x        = "Policy Type",
    y        = "Number of Policies",
    caption  = "TP: Third-party | TPG: TP + Glass | CC: TP + extras | COMP_E/N: Comprehensive"
  )





Distribution of policy types — CC and COMP_E are the dominant coverage structures




The remaining categorical policy attributes are shown as small-multiple bar charts so their distributions can be compared consistently without overloading a single axis.


Show code block
make_bar <- function(var, title, palette = "Blues") {
  motor |>
    count(!!sym(var)) |>
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(!!sym(var), n), y = n, fill = !!sym(var))) +
    geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.9) +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct, 0.1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.22))) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = palette) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Count") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
}

p1 <- make_bar("policy_status",     "Policy Status",     "Blues")
p2 <- make_bar("business_type",     "Business Type",     "Greens")
p3 <- make_bar("payment_frequency", "Payment Frequency", "Oranges")
p4 <- make_bar("bonus_score",       "Bonus Score",       "Purples")

(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Policy and Insured Characteristics",
    caption = "Source: Spanish Motor Insurance Portfolio (2022-2024)",
    theme   = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15))
  )





Policy-level categorical variables: status, business origin, payment frequency, and bonus history




Interpretation:

The portfolio consists predominantly of active policies (89.2%) and annually-paying (81.3%) policies, reflecting a relatively clean operational structure. However, new business accounts for 69.3% of policy-years, which warrants caution when interpreting loss ratios — new business typically carries higher claim propensity due to the absence of renewal selection and policy seasoning effects, and profitability figures may not reflect long-run portfolio behaviour.
The bonus-score distribution is heavily concentrated in “Good” risks (96.4%), with Neutral and Bad segments accounting for just 2.2% and 1.3% respectively. While this may reflect genuine portfolio quality, it severely limits the variable’s discriminatory power. Any comparison of loss experience across bonus-score categories should be treated with caution, as the exposure in non-Good segments is too thin for credible statistical inference.



3.1.2 Vehicle and Geographic Characteristics
Fuel type, municipality type, and circulation area are compact categorical variables, making aligned bar charts suitable for quickly comparing their portfolio shares.


Show code block
p5 <- make_bar("fuel_type",         "Fuel Type",         "Reds")
p6 <- make_bar("municipality_type", "Municipality Type", "GnBu")
p7 <- make_bar("circulation_area",  "Circulation Area",  "Purples")

p5 | p6 | p7





Fuel type, municipality type, and circulation area distributions






3.1.3 Vehicle Brand Composition - Treemap
A treemap is appropriate for vehicle brand because there are many categories; area makes the dominant exposure concentrations visible without requiring a long ranked bar chart.


Show code block
brand_counts <- motor |>
  count(vehicle_brand, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 25) |>
  mutate(pct = n / nrow(motor))

ggplot(
  brand_counts,
  aes(area  = n,
      fill  = n,
      label = paste0(vehicle_brand, "\n", comma(n)))
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white", place = "centre",
    size = 11, reflow = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low  = "#B3CDE3", high = "#08519C",
    name = "Policies", labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 25 Vehicle Brands by Policy Count",
    subtitle = "Renault, Citroen, Peugeot, Volkswagen, Ford, Opel, and Seat form the main exposure base"
  )





Top 25 vehicle brands — area and colour both encode policy count




Interpretation:

The brand exposure is broadly distributed, with no single manufacturer dominating the portfolio. Renault, Citroën, Peugeot, Volkswagen, Ford, Opel, and Seat collectively form the core of the book, each contributing between approximately 28,000 and 34,000 policies. Given their scale, loss experience within these brands will be the primary driver of overall portfolio results, brand-level underwriting attention should therefore focus on whether these high-volume makes exhibit adverse claim frequency or severity, rather than on the tail of smaller brands where credibility is limited.
Premium and near-premium brands: Mercedes, Audi, and BMW, are present but comparatively minor in policy count. While intuition suggests higher repair costs for these vehicles, any separate rating or loading applied to them should be grounded in observed loss evidence from this portfolio rather than assumed from general market benchmarks. Repair cost inflation and parts availability vary across manufacturers and model years, and without claim-level severity data by brand, cost-based assumptions risk being either overstated or misallocated.




3.2 Numerical Variables

3.2.1 Premium Distribution
Most insurance premium distributions are right-skewed because a small proportion of high-risk or high-value policies attract substantially elevated premiums. The histogram shows the mass of annual premium levels, while the density overlay makes the skewness and possible multiple peaks easier to see.


Show code block
motor |>
  filter(total_premium > 0,
         total_premium < quantile(total_premium, 0.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins  = 80, fill = "#1565C0", alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_density(colour = "#0D47A1", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(prefix = "EUR ")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Total Premium (capped at 99th percentile)",
    subtitle = "Right-skewed; most policies pay under EUR 800/year — COMP covers drive the upper tail",
    x        = "Total Annual Premium (EUR)",
    y        = "Density"
  )





Total premium distribution is strongly right-skewed




Interpretation:

Most policyholders pay under EUR 300 annually, suggesting the portfolio is predominantly low-premium, high-volume in nature, which is a business model sensitive to loss frequency rather than severity. The right tail indicates a smaller segment of comprehensively covered, likely higher-value vehicles where individual claim severity matters more.



The near-bimodal shape implies the portfolio is effectively serving two distinct customer segments with different coverage needs and risk profiles, yet they are being analysed and possibly priced as a single book. This has implications for profitability monitoring, aggregate loss ratios may mask divergent performance between the low-premium mass and the high-premium tail.
From a business perspective, growth strategy and retention efforts should distinguish between these segments, as the economics of acquiring and retaining a EUR 150 policy versus a EUR 700 policy are materially different in terms of expense ratio, claims handling cost, and margin contribution.



3.2.2 Loss Ratio Distribution with Statistical Test
The loss ratio (incurred losses ÷ earned premium) is the primary profitability metric in non-life insurance. A value below 1.0 indicates underwriting profit; above 1.0 indicates a loss. I test whether the portfolio median loss ratio is significantly below the break-even threshold of 1.0 using a one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test, since the distribution is non-normal.


Show code block
motor_lr <- motor |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), loss_ratio >= 0,
         loss_ratio <= 5, total_premium > 0)

set.seed(42)
gghistostats(
  data         = motor_lr |> slice_sample(n = 50000),
  x            = loss_ratio,
  test.value   = 1,
  type         = "nonparametric",
  normal.curve = TRUE,
  title        = "Distribution of Policy-Level Loss Ratio",
  xlab         = "Loss Ratio (Incurred / Premium)",
  bar.fill     = "#EF9A9A"
)





Loss ratio distribution with embedded Wilcoxon test against break-even (LR = 1)




Interpretation:

The distribution is heavily zero-inflated: the large mass at zero reflects the majority of policies that incur no claims, and exhibits a long right tail driven by a minority of policies with large individual losses. The Wilcoxon test confirms that the typical policy-year sits below break-even, but aggregate profitability should be read from the portfolio loss ratio itself: incurred losses are about 70% of premium, leaving the book profitable while still exposed to tail volatility.
From an insurance and reinsurance perspective, the zero mass and long right tail must be read together. The portfolio can be profitable on average while still exposing the insurer to retained earnings volatility if a small number of claim-bearing policy-years dominate incurred losses. The diagnostics below therefore separate attritional behaviour from large-loss concentration before moving into segment comparisons.



Show code block
claim_tail <- motor |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(total_incurred)) |>
  mutate(
    rank = row_number(),
    claim_policy_share = rank / n(),
    incurred_share = cumsum(total_incurred) / sum(total_incurred)
  )

tail_summary <- tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Aggregate loss ratio",
    "Policy-years with at least one claim",
    "Exposure-adjusted claim frequency",
    "Portfolio average severity",
    "Top 1% of claim-bearing policy-years: incurred share",
    "Top 5% of claim-bearing policy-years: incurred share",
    "Top 10% of claim-bearing policy-years: incurred share",
    "99th percentile incurred loss, claim-bearing rows",
    "99.5th percentile incurred loss, claim-bearing rows",
    "99.9th percentile incurred loss, claim-bearing rows",
    "Maximum policy-year incurred loss"
  ),
  Value = c(
    percent(sum(motor$total_incurred) / sum(motor$total_premium), 0.1),
    percent(mean(motor$has_claim), 0.1),
    percent(sum(motor$total_claims) / sum(motor$total_exposure), 0.1),
    dollar(sum(motor$total_incurred) / sum(motor$total_claims), prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1),
    percent(sum(claim_tail$total_incurred[claim_tail$rank <= ceiling(nrow(claim_tail) * 0.01)]) / sum(claim_tail$total_incurred), 0.1),
    percent(sum(claim_tail$total_incurred[claim_tail$rank <= ceiling(nrow(claim_tail) * 0.05)]) / sum(claim_tail$total_incurred), 0.1),
    percent(sum(claim_tail$total_incurred[claim_tail$rank <= ceiling(nrow(claim_tail) * 0.10)]) / sum(claim_tail$total_incurred), 0.1),
    dollar(quantile(claim_tail$total_incurred, 0.99), prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1),
    dollar(quantile(claim_tail$total_incurred, 0.995), prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1),
    dollar(quantile(claim_tail$total_incurred, 0.999), prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1),
    dollar(max(claim_tail$total_incurred), prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1)
  )
)

knitr::kable(tail_summary, caption = "Tail Diagnostics for Portfolio Loss Volatility")
